summary: Research multipath transports, platform network APIs and prior art for LIVETAP Bond

report.summary: Only one transport family can actually deliver LIVETAP Bond today: application-level packet bonding over plain UDP, on the SRTLA model, terminated by a relay we own. Every kernel-level option is closed — Android GKI kernels (android15-6.6 and android16-6.12) ship no CONFIG_MPTCP at all, Windows has no MPTCP implementation, and Apple exposes MPTCP only through URLSession/Network.framework with an entitlement, never as a raw socket. Multipath QUIC is still an Internet-Draft (draft-ietf-quic-multipath-21, in the RFC Editor queue) and none of msquic, cloudflare/quiche, quinn or lsquic implement it. SRT's own 1.5 bonding cannot aggregate bandwidth: broadcast duplicates, backup fails over, and "balancing" — the only aggregating mode — is still marked UNDER DEVELOPMENT in Haivision's own docs. The unprivileged path that works on both targets is: Android ConnectivityManager.requestNetwork + Network.bindSocket per path (CHANGE_NETWORK_STATE, a normal permission), and per-source-address UDP sockets in Electron's Node process.

options.name: MPTCP (RFC 8684) — Android
options.androidSupport: NONE. CONFIG_MPTCP is absent from android15-6.6 and android16-6.12 arm64 gki_defconfig. Stock devices cannot open an IPPROTO_MPTCP (262) socket. mptcp-nexus/android exists only as a custom AOSP/kernel port.
options.natTraversal: Client-initiated subflows traverse NAT, but middleboxes that strip MPTCP options force silent fallback to plain TCP (RFC 8684 fallback).
options.verdict: reject — not a shipping-app option on Android at any privilege level; it needs a replacement kernel, which we cannot require of users.

options.name: MPTCP — Electron desktop (Windows / macOS / Linux)
options.androidSupport: n/a
options.desktopSupport: Windows: no MPTCP implementation in any Windows or Windows Server release. macOS: no public socket API — MPTCP only via URLSessionConfiguration.multipathServiceType / NWParameters.MultipathServiceType, i.e. HTTP(S) only, no UDP, no RTMP, no SRT. Linux: socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, IPPROTO_MPTCP) works from v5.6 (v6.1+ realistically), but additional subflows require endpoints configured via `ip mptcp endpoint` or a userspace path manager over netlink — admin/CAP_NET_ADMIN, not something an unprivileged Electron app can do.
options.natTraversal: Same as above; fallback-to-TCP on option-stripping middleboxes.
options.verdict: reject — dead on Windows, API-locked on macOS, root-gated on Linux; and it is reliable in-order TCP, so one bad path head-of-line-blocks the live stream.

options.name: MPTCP — iOS (for completeness)
options.iosSupport: handover and interactive service types work with no extra steps; aggregate (the only bandwidth-adding mode) requires the com.apple.developer.networking.multipath entitlement. All of it is reachable only through URLSession / Network.framework — there is no raw MPTCP socket, so it cannot carry SRT, RTMP or our own UDP framing.
options.androidSupport: n/a
options.verdict: reject — even where MPTCP exists and is mature, the API surface excludes live-video transport entirely.

options.name: Multipath QUIC (draft-ietf-quic-multipath)
options.license: spec: IETF Trust / Revised BSD for code components
options.iosSupport: only via xquic or picoquic built into the app
options.androidSupport: only via xquic or picoquic built into the app (NDK); no platform support anywhere
options.natTraversal: Good in principle: each path is a client-initiated UDP 4-tuple to the same server, explicit Path IDs, per-path packet number spaces. Survives CGNAT.
options.verdict: prototype only, not for v1 — draft-21 dated March 2026 is in the RFC Editor queue after 9 years and 21 drafts; the wire format has churned repeatedly and we would be chasing it.

options.name: msquic (Microsoft)
options.androidSupport: no multipath
options.evidence: https://github.com/microsoft/msquic/discussions/4890 — maintainer nibanks, 4 Mar 2025: "We do not yet support multipath QUIC, nor do we have a timeline to add support officially."
options.verdict: reject — explicit maintainer statement that multipath is not supported and not scheduled.

options.name: cloudflare/quiche
options.androidSupport: no multipath
options.verdict: reject — request open seven years with no implementation. Note: literature conflating 'quiche' sometimes means Google's quiche, a different codebase.

options.name: quinn (Rust)
options.androidSupport: no multipath
options.evidence: https://github.com/quinn-rs/quinn/issues/224 ("Implement support for multipath", open since 5 Feb 2019)
options.verdict: reject — tracking issue only, no implementation.

options.name: lsquic (LiteSpeed)
options.androidSupport: no multipath
options.evidence: Absent from every multipath implementation list surveyed, incl. https://quicwg.org/implementations and https://github.com/mmmarcos/awesome-quic
options.verdict: reject — no evidence of any multipath work.

options.name: picoquic
options.iosSupport: builds (FreeBSD/iOS tested) but no product integration
options.androidSupport: C, NDK-buildable in principle; no known shipping mobile use
options.verdict: reject for product, useful as a conformance reference — it is the draft author's testbed, deliberately minimal, not an engineering-supported product library.

options.name: tquic (Tencent)
options.maturity: production QUIC; multipath on a stale draft
options.androidSupport: Rust + C FFI, buildable
options.evidence: https://github.com/Tencent/tquic ; https://github.com/Tencent/tquic/discussions/379 — multipath based on draft-ietf-quic-multipath-05, "you currently need to use tquic for both the client and the server"
options.verdict: prototype at most — multipath pinned to draft-05 and tquic-to-tquic only, so we would own both ends anyway and gain nothing over our own framing.

options.name: xquic (Alibaba)
options.iosSupport: shipped in Taobao iOS at scale
options.androidSupport: shipped in Taobao Android at scale — the only MPQUIC stack with real mobile production mileage
options.desktopSupport: cross-platform C; server-side used with Alibaba CDN
options.evidence: https://github.com/alibaba/xquic ; XLINK SIGCOMM 2021 https://conferences.sigcomm.org/sigcomm/2021/files/papers/3452296.3472893.pdf ; https://github.com/alibaba/XQUIC/pull/287 (multipath draft-19 support, opened 13 Jan 2026)
options.verdict: prototype — the single credible MPQUIC option, but it is tuned for QoE-driven HTTP/3 video download, docs are largely Chinese, and we would still be shipping a draft protocol against a relay we build ourselves.

options.name: SRT native connection bonding (SRT 1.5+, socket groups)
options.maturity: production for redundancy/failover; aggregation still unreleased
options.androidSupport: libsrt builds via NDK, but must be compiled with ENABLE_BONDING=ON — off by default, so ffmpeg/OBS/most prebuilt libsrt binaries lack it entirely
options.desktopSupport: same; needs a native module in Electron
options.natTraversal: fine — UDP, caller-initiated to our listener; SRTO_GROUPCONNECT on our relay accepts the group handshake extension
options.evidence: https://github.com/Haivision/srt/blob/master/docs/features/socket-groups.md — "Balancing (**UNDER DEVELOPMENT!**)" ; https://github.com/Haivision/srt/issues/1120 (load-balancing implementation and docs still unchecked) ; https://github.com/Haivision/srt/releases/tag/v1.5.0 (ENABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BONDING renamed ENABLE_BONDING, off by default)
options.verdict: adopt for failover only, reject for aggregation — broadcast duplicates the stream on every link (N× uplink for 1× bitrate), backup is hot-standby failover, and balancing is the only mode that adds bandwidth and has never shipped.

options.name: SRTLA (BELABOX) — the wire protocol
options.maturity: de-facto industry standard for bonded IRL streaming
options.iosSupport: proven — Moblin implements an SRTLA client in an unprivileged App Store app
options.androidSupport: proven — Brix implements SRT+SRTLA from scratch in Kotlin on top of RootEncoder (the same encoder LIVETAP already ships), no root; IRL Pro likewise
options.desktopSupport: Linux reference implementation; runs on Windows only via WSL1. A desktop client needs per-source-address UDP sockets, which Node/Electron can do.
options.natTraversal: Excellent — every link is a client-initiated UDP flow to the same relay IP:port; the receiver correlates links into a group via a 256-byte connection ID exchanged in SRTLA_REG1(0x9200)/REG2(0x9201)/REG3(0x9202). No inbound ports, no STUN, works behind CGNAT.
options.evidence: https://github.com/BELABOX/srtla ; https://github.com/BELABOX/srtla/blob/main/common.h (SRTLA_TYPE_KEEPALIVE 0x9000, SRTLA_TYPE_ACK 0x9100, REG1/2/3 0x9200/0x9201/0x9202, REG_ERR 0x9210, REG_NGP 0x9211, REG_NAK 0x9212, MTU 1500, SRTLA_ID_LEN 256) ; https://github.com/0rb1ta/Brix ; https://github.com/eerimoq/moblin
options.verdict: adopt the protocol, not the code — it is the closest existing art, already implemented by unprivileged mobile apps, and it is a small protocol: per-link in-flight counters plus a dynamic per-link window, traffic split proportional to measured capacity.

options.name: BELABOX srtla_rec (the reference receiver)
options.androidSupport: n/a
options.evidence: https://github.com/BELABOX/srtla — README: "The server component - srtla_rec - in this repository is unsupported, no longer under development"; also requires a patched libsrt because upstream SRT "causes excessive retransmissions when packets arrive out of order"
options.verdict: reject — abandoned upstream, needs a forked libsrt, and AGPL-3.0 on a network service means running it on our relay triggers the source-disclosure obligation for the whole relay.

options.name: Maintained SRTLA receivers (alternatives to srtla_rec)
options.license: mixed — go-irl (Go), irlserver/irl-srt-server (C, SLS fork, needs IRL's patched libsrt), irlserver/srtla_send (Rust sender), MediaMTX PR #5811 (MIT project, PR NOT merged)
options.androidSupport: n/a
options.evidence: https://github.com/e04/go-irl ; https://github.com/irlserver/irl-srt-server ; https://github.com/irlserver/srtla_send ; https://github.com/bluenviron/mediamtx/pull/5811 — open, unmerged as of 5 Sep 2026; maintainer aler9 objects that SRTLA is "completely unstandardized"
options.verdict: prototype against these, ship our own — check each project's license before borrowing a line; treat them as interop targets and test fixtures.

options.name: RIST bonding / load-sharing (librist)
options.license: BSD-2-Clause — the cleanest licence in this whole table
options.iosSupport: C library, buildable; Moblin already supports RIST alongside SRTLA
options.androidSupport: C library, NDK-buildable; no widely-shipped Android integration found
options.desktopSupport: cross-platform C, usable from Electron via a native module
options.natTraversal: UDP, caller-initiated; same CGNAT-friendly shape as SRT
options.evidence: https://code.videolan.org/rist/librist ; https://www.rist.tv/articles-and-deep-dives/2020/6/16/rist-bonding-and-load-sharing-demystified (load sharing splits packets across links rather than duplicating) ; https://code.videolan.org/rist/librist/-/issues/47
options.verdict: prototype — the only option that gives real load-sharing under a permissive licence with an actual published spec; weaker than SRTLA on mobile ecosystem and field-proven IRL use.

options.name: WebRTC / WHIP (RFC 9725) as a bonding transport
options.maturity: WHIP is a 2025 Standards-Track RFC; multipath does not exist in it
options.androidSupport: single path only
options.natTraversal: Best-in-class (ICE/STUN/TURN) — but that solves a problem we do not have, since our relay has a public address.
options.evidence: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9725.txt (WHIP, March 2025 — HTTP signalling for WebRTC ingest, nothing about multipath) ; https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/RTCIceCandidatePairStats and getSelectedCandidatePair() — ICE converges on exactly one selected candidate pair carrying media
options.verdict: reject as a bonding transport — ICE picks one candidate pair and sends media on it; there is no standard aggregation, and WHIP is signalling only. Keep WHIP in mind for relay→platform egress, not for client→relay.

options.name: Application-level bonding over plain UDP (our own sequencing + FEC/ARQ)
options.maturity: the approach every shipping bonded-IRL product actually uses
options.iosSupport: n/a for LIVETAP today, but Moblin proves it
options.androidSupport: YES, unprivileged: ConnectivityManager.requestNetwork(NetworkRequest with TRANSPORT_CELLULAR / TRANSPORT_WIFI / TRANSPORT_ETHERNET) + Network.bindSocket(DatagramSocket) gives one socket per path while another path stays the system default. Needs android.permission.CHANGE_NETWORK_STATE (normal, install-time) plus INTERNET/ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE, and a foreground service.
options.desktopSupport: YES, unprivileged, with one caveat per OS. Windows Vista+ uses the strong host send model, so dgram.bind({address}) genuinely selects the interface. macOS: bind by source address, or IP_BOUND_IF via a native module. Linux: binding the source IP alone is NOT enough — you need SO_BINDTODEVICE (unprivileged since kernel 5.7, commit c427bfec18f2) or policy routing (root). Node's dgram exposes only `localAddress` and no setsockopt, so Linux needs a small native addon.
options.natTraversal: Trivial — all paths are client-initiated UDP flows to one relay IP:port. No STUN, no TURN, no inbound ports, CGNAT-safe.
options.evidence: https://developer.android.com/reference/android/net/Network (bindSocket / openConnection enable multipath data transfer on a non-default network) ; https://developer.android.com/develop/connectivity/network-ops/reading-network-state ; https://nodejs.org/api/dgram.html ; https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/35769 (no SO_BINDTODEVICE in dgram) ; https://git.zx2c4.com/linux-rng/commit/net?id=c427bfec18f2190b8f4718785ee8ed2db4f84ee6 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Host_model
options.verdict: adopt — this is the only layer where both an unprivileged Android app and an unprivileged Electron app can genuinely use several paths at once today.

hardConstraints: MPTCP is impossible on stock Android. CONFIG_MPTCP appears nowhere in Google's GKI defconfigs for android15-6.6 or android16-6.12 (arm64 or x86). No socket(…, IPPROTO_MPTCP=262) will succeed. Root does not help — it needs a different kernel. Source: https://android.googlesource.com/kernel/common/+/refs/heads/android16-6.12/arch/arm64/configs/gki_defconfig

Windows has no MPTCP implementation in any release, Windows Server 2025 included. Any MPTCP design kills the Electron app on its largest platform outright. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multipath_TCP , https://github.com/multipath-tcp/mptcp/issues/76

Even on Linux, an unprivileged process cannot create MPTCP subflows. Opening the socket is opt-in and unprivileged, but additional paths require endpoints configured with `ip mptcp endpoint` or a netlink userspace path manager (mptcpd) — admin-level. Source: https://docs.kernel.org/networking/mptcp.html

Apple exposes MPTCP only through URLSession / Network.framework. There is no raw MPTCP socket on iOS or macOS, so it cannot carry SRT, RTMP, or our own UDP framing at all; and the aggregate service type additionally needs the com.apple.developer.networking.multipath entitlement. Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/entitlements/com.apple.developer.networking.multipath

MPTCP is reliable, in-order TCP. A single stalled or lossy path head-of-line-blocks the whole live stream. Even in a world where it were available everywhere, it is the wrong shape for live video; this is why every bonded-IRL product uses UDP.

mptcpize cannot rescue us: it is an LD_PRELOAD shim over glibc socket(), so it does not work on Go binaries, and it is irrelevant on Android (bionic) and non-existent on Windows/macOS. Source: https://github.com/multipath-tcp/mptcpd

Multipath QUIC is not a finished standard. draft-ietf-quic-multipath-21 (17 Mar 2026) sits in the RFC Editor queue after 21 drafts and nine years; the draft author himself wrote in 2024 that the WG "had to go back to the drawing board". Source: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-quic-multipath/ , https://www.privateoctopus.com/2024/02/28/long-slow-path-to-quic-multipath.html

No mainstream QUIC library implements multipath. msquic: maintainer on record 4 Mar 2025, "We do not yet support multipath QUIC, nor do we have a timeline". cloudflare/quiche: issue #278 open since 2019. quinn: issue #224 open since 2019. lsquic: nothing. The only implementations are picoquic (research), tquic (pinned to draft-05, tquic-to-tquic only) and xquic.

SRT's built-in connection bonding cannot aggregate bandwidth in any released version. Broadcast sends the full stream on every link (N× uplink for 1× bitrate), main/backup is hot-standby failover, and the only aggregating mode — balancing — is literally labelled "(**UNDER DEVELOPMENT!**)" in Haivision's own socket-groups.md, with its implementation and documentation still unchecked on roadmap issue #1120. Source: https://github.com/Haivision/srt/blob/master/docs/features/socket-groups.md

SRT bonding is compiled out by default. ENABLE_BONDING defaults to OFF, so stock libsrt in ffmpeg, OBS and most Android/NDK prebuilds has no group support — we would have to ship our own libsrt build on every platform. Source: https://github.com/Haivision/srt/releases/tag/v1.5.0

The BELABOX SRTLA reference receiver is abandoned and AGPL-3.0. Its README states srtla_rec is "unsupported, no longer under development", and it requires a patched libsrt because upstream SRT "causes excessive retransmissions when packets arrive out of order". AGPL on a relay triggers network-use source disclosure — we cannot run that code on a LIVETAP-owned relay without open-sourcing it. Source: https://github.com/BELABOX/srtla

There is no SRTLA specification. MediaMTX's maintainer refused to merge the SRTLA receiver PR (#5811, still open 5 Sep 2026) precisely because SRTLA is "completely unstandardized" — the only normative artefact is BELABOX's AGPL C source. Any clean-room reimplementation must be written from observed wire behaviour and the published constants, and pinned by interop tests against Moblin / IRL Pro / Brix.

WebRTC cannot bond. ICE converges on exactly one selected candidate pair and sends media over it; there is no standardized bandwidth aggregation across candidate pairs in libwebrtc. WHIP (RFC 9725, March 2025) is HTTP signalling for WebRTC ingest and says nothing about multipath. Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9725.txt

One Android phone realistically yields at most Wi-Fi + one cellular path (+ USB Ethernet/tether). Dual-SIM devices are overwhelmingly DSDS — only one SIM carries data at a time; DSDA with simultaneous dual data is device- and carrier-gated. This is exactly why Moblin shipped Moblink, which turns spare phones into extra bonding links over WebSocket control + UDP forwarding. Plan for cross-device bonding, not multiple 5G paths from one handset. Source: https://github.com/datagutt/moblink-rust

Node.js cannot bind a UDP socket to a network interface. dgram exposes only `localAddress`, with no setsockopt and no SO_BINDTODEVICE (nodejs/node#35769). On Windows this is survivable — Vista+ uses the strong host send model, so a source-address bind really does select the interface — but on Linux, source-IP binding without policy routing is silently ignored by the routing table. Linux Electron needs a native addon calling SO_BINDTODEVICE (unprivileged since kernel 5.7) or root-configured source routing, which is the same constraint BELABOX's README imposes on srtla_send.
report.recommendation:
Build LIVETAP Bond as a clean-room, wire-compatible SRTLA v2 client and relay, carrying SRT as the inner reliability layer, and do not adopt any kernel-level or draft-standard multipath transport for v1.

Concretely:
1. Transport: plain UDP, one socket per path, all paths to one relay IP:port. Reimplement the SRTLA v2 framing from the published constants (KEEPALIVE 0x9000, ACK 0x9100, REG1/REG2/REG3 0x9200/0x9201/0x9202, REG_ERR/NGP/NAK 0x9210/0x9211/0x9212, 256-byte group ID, 1500 MTU) rather than linking BELABOX's AGPL code. Wire compatibility buys us instant interop with Moblin, IRL Pro and Brix as free field-test clients, and lets LIVETAP users point existing hardware at our relay.
2. Scheduler: per-link in-flight counter plus a dynamic per-link window, split proportional to measured capacity — SRTLA's own model, which is the one with real IRL mileage. Add a duplicate-on-last-link mode for the final N ms of keyframes rather than blanket FEC; FEC on a bonded link mostly wastes the uplink you just aggregated.
3. Inner protocol: libsrt (MPL-2.0) with lossmaxttl raised (10–50) and an explicit latency budget, since bonded delivery is inherently out-of-order. Budget engineering time to either carry BELABOX's out-of-order retransmission patch forward on our own libsrt fork or fix it upstream — this is a known, load-bearing gotcha, not a detail.
4. Android: ConnectivityManager.requestNetwork per transport + Network.bindSocket on each DatagramSocket, CHANGE_NETWORK_STATE in the manifest, all inside a foreground service. Brix already proves a Kotlin SRTLA client on RootEncoder works unprivileged, on the same encoder LIVETAP ships.
5. Electron: do the bonding in the main process with node dgram, one socket bound per source address. Ship a small native addon for Linux SO_BINDTODEVICE and macOS IP_BOUND_IF; Windows needs neither.
6. Relay: write our own receiver. Treat go-irl, irl-srt-server and MediaMTX PR #5811 as interop targets and test fixtures, not as dependencies — check each licence before borrowing.
7. Park, don't pursue: revisit multipath QUIC (via xquic, the only stack with real mobile production mileage) only once the draft is a published RFC and a second independent mobile-capable implementation interops with it. Keep SRT's native main/backup groups as a cheap failover fallback for single-path users. Evaluate librist (BSD-2-Clause, real load-sharing, an actual published spec in VSF TR-06-2) as the licensing-clean plan B if SRTLA's lack of a specification becomes a legal or maintenance problem.
uncertainties: Whether draft-ietf-quic-multipath has been assigned an RFC number. As of the sources checked (Sept 2026) the datatracker shows draft-21 dated 17 Mar 2026 in the RFC Editor queue with no number published. If it has since been issued as an RFC, that changes the timeline argument but not the library-availability one.

Whether any individual Android OEM enables CONFIG_MPTCP in its device kernel despite GKI not doing so. I found none, but I verified Google's common-kernel defconfigs, not every vendor tree. It would not change the recommendation — we cannot ship a feature that works on an unknown subset of devices.

Exact per-path behaviour of Brix's Kotlin SRTLA implementation — the README does not name the Android APIs it uses for per-network binding, so my claim that it uses requestNetwork/bindSocket is inference from the platform constraints, not from its source. Worth reading Brix's source directly before we design our own binding layer. Note also Brix is GPL-3.0, so read it for understanding, do not copy from it.

Current SRT balancing-mode status in unreleased branches. socket-groups.md and roadmap issue #1120 both still show it incomplete, but I did not read the v1.5.7 changelog line by line; confirm against https://github.com/Haivision/srt/releases/tag/v1.5.7 before quoting this to anyone outside the team.

librist's bonding maturity on mobile. The licence (BSD-2-Clause) and the load-sharing design are well documented, but I found no shipping Android integration, so its real-world behaviour on flapping cellular links is unproven for our use case in a way SRTLA's is not.
Whether Apple would grant the multipath entitlement to LIVETAP if we ever ship iOS. Moot for the current recommendation, since the API cannot carry our transport regardless.

verdict.claim: Build LIVETAP Bond as a clean-room, wire-compatible SRTLA v2 client and relay carrying SRT inside, with libsrt (lossmaxttl 10–50) as the inner protocol, a self-written relay, RootEncoder/Brix-style Android bonding, and Node dgram bonding in Electron — adopting no kernel-level or draft multipath transport for v1.
verdict.reasoning:
The HARD CONSTRAINTS are almost all correct — I verified them and they survive. CONFIG_MPTCP genuinely does not appear in android16-6.12 arm64 gki_defconfig. libsrt is genuinely MPL-2.0. BELABOX/srtla is genuinely AGPL-3.0 with srtla_rec "unsupported, no longer under development and not suitable for production deployment." The MediaMTX maintainer genuinely wrote that SRTLA "is completely unstandardized and compatible with an unmaintained library only" on PR #5811, still open. Multipath QUIC is genuinely not an RFC. The strategic direction (UDP, SRTLA-shaped, not MPTCP/MPQUIC) is sound.

But the seven numbered recommendations are refuted on five independently sufficient grounds.

(1) THE LICENSING PREMISE IS FALSE — refutes items 1 and 6. The plan exists to dodge an AGPL problem that has a permissive path around it, which the researcher never checked. Moblin is MIT (https://github.com/eerimoq/moblin/blob/main/LICENSE — "MIT License", (c) 2023 Erik Moqvist) and contains a complete, field-proven SRTLA client. irl-srt-server is MIT ("The MIT License (MIT), Copyright (c) 2019-2020 Edward.Wu, Copyright (c) 2021 rstular") and is a working SRTLA receiver. The SRT patches SRTLA requires are already maintained permissively at https://github.com/irlserver/srt branch `belabox`, MPL-2.0. So a clean-room reimplementation from constants (item 1), writing our own receiver (item 6), and forking libsrt ourselves (item 3) are all unnecessary cost. The researcher correctly identified BELABOX as AGPL and then generalised that to the whole ecosystem.

(2) SRTLA IS NOT TRANSPORT-AGNOSTIC — refutes item 2's scheduler. BELABOX's README states the NAKs sent by SRT are what srtla uses to balance traffic between the links. Item 2 describes the scheduler as "per-link in-flight counter plus a dynamic per-link window, split proportional to measured capacity" and omits the SRT-NAK feedback loop entirely. An implementation built to item 2's written description will not balance links. SRTLA requires deep-parsing SRT control packets on the return path.

(3) ITEM 3'S TUNING IS BACKWARDS AND WOULD BREAK BONDING. irl-srt-server documents the actual requirement: "SRTLA bonded connections require special SRT patches that disable dynamic reorder tolerance and periodic NAK reports." Per Haivision's API-socket-options.md, SRTO_LOSSMAXTTL *is* the dynamic reorder-tolerance mechanism ("the Reorder Tolerance is set to the value of the interval between latest sequence and this packet's sequence, but not more than the value set by SRTO_LOSSMAXTTL"). Item 3 says raise it to 10–50, i.e. turn up the very mechanism the patch disables. SRTO_NAKREPORT ("turns on repeated sending of loss reports") must be OFF, since repeated NAKs corrupt the balancer's input signal — item 3 never mentions it. Item 3 also misplaces the patch: BELABOX says "Our patched SRT library should be used on the receiver," not the client.

(4) ITEMS 3 AND 4 ARE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE. Item 4 cites Brix as proof, but Brix's README says "The SRT and SRTLA client is written from scratch in Kotlin; it is not a wrapper around libsrt." RootEncoder (Apache-2.0), which LIVETAP already ships, is likewise "all code written in Java/Kotlin" — its SRT module is a native Kotlin implementation. There is no libsrt on LIVETAP's Android path, so there is no socket on which to set SRTO_LOSSMAXTTL or SRTO_NAKREPORT and no BELABOX patch to carry forward. Item 4's own evidence disproves item 3. Also: Brix is GPL-3.0, so LIVETAP can no more copy it than it can copy BELABOX; it is field-tested "exclusively on a Samsung S21 (Exynos 2100, Android 15)" — one device, not fleet proof; and its own caveats ("At 1080p the phone reaches the `critical` thermal state in about six minutes", "Streaming costs 6-10 W", Moblink "untested in production") are product-level constraints the recommendation never surfaces.

(5) WIRE COMPATIBILITY AND A COMMERCIAL RELAY ARE IN DIRECT CONTRADICTION. BELABOX's README states the setup "doesn't implement authentication or encryption." SRTLA registration is REG1 (sender-random group ID) → REG2 (receiver fills the last half) → REG3, with no credential anywhere. Auth can only ride in the SRT streamid, readable only after the group and per-link socket state are already allocated. A metered LIVETAP-owned relay must therefore allocate state for unauthenticated UDP senders — and item 1 cannot fix this, because adding a registration credential breaks the Moblin/IRL Pro interop that is item 1's entire justification.

Two further errors. Item 6 misses that the relay can never serve both ingest types from one stack: "Direct SRT served with SRTLA patches drops packets, while SRTLA served without the patches produces spurious retransmissions" — which is why irl-srt-server runs separate publisher ports. Item 5 understates Electron scope badly: there is no SRT in Node, LIVETAP's desktop currently does RTMP only, and libsrt owns its own UDP socket with no sendto hook, so the real datapath is a native libsrt addon on all three platforms → loopback UDP → per-packet JS bonding → N dgram sockets. "A small native addon for Linux and macOS; Windows needs neither" is wrong about scope. (nodejs/node#35769 is closed as not planned, so that gap is permanent; the Windows strong-host-send claim does check out as a default, though it is per-interface configurable back to weak host.)

Minor correction in the researcher's favour: draft-ietf-quic-multipath-21 is not "in the RFC Editor queue" — datatracker shows IESG state "Waiting for AD Go-Ahead::AD Followup", so it has no RFC number at all. Park-it is right, for a stronger reason than stated. Also, "no specification" is slightly overstated: BELABOX's README does document the v2 registration exchange, group-ID construction, error types and the in-flight/dynamic-window scheduler.
verdict.correction:
The direction survives; the plan does not. Keep: UDP, one socket per path to one relay, SRTLA-shaped framing, no MPTCP, no multipath QUIC. Change five things.

1. Stop clean-rooming. The AGPL trap is real but avoidable — you never had to reimplement. Adopt or fork the MIT/MPL stack instead: Moblin (MIT) for the client-side SRTLA reference, irl-srt-server (MIT) as the relay, irlserver/srt branch `belabox` (MPL-2.0) for the SRT patches already carried forward. Reserve clean-room effort for the scheduler you actually want to differentiate on. Note MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft: modified libsrt files must be published, which is fine for a relay in a way AGPL is not.

2. Fix the scheduler model before writing code. SRTLA's balancer is driven by snooping SRT NAKs on the return path, not by measured capacity alone. Your sender must parse SRT control packets. Budget for that; it is the core of the thing.

3. Invert item 3's tuning. The receiver needs dynamic reorder tolerance DISABLED and periodic NAK reports (SRTO_NAKREPORT) OFF. Raising SRTO_LOSSMAXTTL to 10–50 turns up the mechanism that must be pinned down, and leaving NAKREPORT on feeds the balancer duplicate loss signals. Verify whether socket options alone suffice or the fork is genuinely required — if options suffice, item 3's fork budget disappears.

4. Resolve the Android contradiction. LIVETAP ships RootEncoder, whose SRT is Kotlin, not libsrt — so there is no socket to tune and no patch to carry. Pick one: write a Kotlin SRT+SRTLA client (Brix's path, ~a full protocol implementation, and you cannot copy Brix because it is GPL-3.0), or replace RootEncoder's SRT module with an NDK libsrt build. Neither is costed in the current plan. Also treat Brix's six-minutes-to-critical-thermal at 1080p on an S21 as a product constraint, not a footnote.

5. Design relay auth up front, and accept the trade. SRTLA has no authentication or encryption, and wire compatibility forbids adding any at the registration layer without losing the Moblin/IRL Pro interop you are buying. Either accept unauthenticated group-state allocation and defend it with rate limits, per-IP group caps and short registration timeouts with streamid auth immediately behind it — or add a LIVETAP-only registration extension and give up the "point existing hardware at our relay" selling point. The plan cannot have both, and currently assumes it can.

Also correct: the relay needs two ingest paths permanently (patched SRT for SRTLA, stock SRT for direct), and Electron needs a native libsrt addon on all three platforms plus a loopback hop, not a small shim on two.

report.summary: Android permits exactly what LIVETAP Bond needs, but only in one narrow shape: ConnectivityManager.requestNetwork() with a transport-specific NetworkRequest, held open for the life of the broadcast, plus Network.bindSocket() on a fresh, UNCONNECTED socket per path. That combination genuinely holds Wi-Fi and cellular up at the same time and sends on both, needs only CHANGE_NETWORK_STATE (protection level "normal", auto-granted at install, no runtime prompt), and is what Speedify ships on Android today. Everything that sounds more advanced is closed: LTE+5G on one SIM is one PDN and cannot be two paths, two internet-bearing Wi-Fi networks is privileged-apps-only, dual-SIM dual-data has no public binding API, and MPTCP is not exposed on Android. The realistic path count on a stock phone is TWO (Wi-Fi + one cellular), three only with a USB-Ethernet adapter. The sharpest schedule risks are not networking at all: bindSocket() throws on an already-connected socket (so RootEncoder's RTMP socket cannot be retrofitted — Bond must own its own sockets), and the foreground-service type you pick decides whether the broadcast survives past 6 hours.

options.name: requestNetwork(NetworkRequest) + Network.bindSocket() — per-socket path binding
options.verdict: ADOPT. This is the only supported way to send on two networks at once, it is stable since API 21/23, and the permission is free. Build Bond on exactly this.
options.androidSupport: Full. requestNetwork() API 21; bindSocket(Socket) API 21, bindSocket(DatagramSocket) API 22, bindSocket(FileDescriptor) API 23. Unchanged through Android 13/14/15/16. Hold one NetworkRequest per path (addTransportType(TRANSPORT_WIFI) / TRANSPORT_CELLULAR + addCapability(NET_CAPABILITY_INTERNET)); each outstanding request keeps its network alive independently of which one is the system default. Per javadoc, a bound socket's traffic goes on that Network 'irrespective of any process-wide network binding set by ConnectivityManager#bindProcessToNetwork'.
options.iosSupport: N/A (this lens is Android). iOS equivalent is NWParameters.requiredInterfaceType on Network.framework — different API, different constraints.
options.desktopSupport: N/A. Desktop Electron binds by source-IP/interface instead; no ConnectivityManager equivalent.
options.natTraversal: Irrelevant on this leg — the phone is the client dialing out to the LIVETAP relay. Each bound socket gets its own public 5-tuple through its own carrier/home NAT; the relay sees N distinct source addresses and must correlate them by an application-level session ID, not by IP.
options.license: Android platform API, Apache 2.0 (AOSP). No third-party dependency.

options.name: CHANGE_NETWORK_STATE permission (the cost of the above)
options.verdict: ADOPT, and note the good news: it is protection level 'normal', granted at install with no user prompt and no runtime dialog. Bond costs nothing in permission UX.
options.androidSupport: API 1+. requestNetwork() javadoc: 'requires the caller to hold either the android.Manifest.permission#CHANGE_NETWORK_STATE permission or the ability to modify system settings as determined by android.provider.Settings.System#canWrite'. ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE (also normal) is needed to read capabilities and to call getMultipathPreference(). Neither is a runtime permission; users cannot revoke them.

options.name: ConnectivityManager.bindProcessToNetwork()
options.verdict: REJECT for Bond. It is process-wide and therefore single-path by construction — it routes ALL future sockets in the process onto one network, which is the opposite of bonding. Per-socket bindSocket() explicitly overrides it, so it is also redundant.
options.androidSupport: API 23+. Useful only as a debugging lever or a deliberate single-path fallback mode.

options.name: ConnectivityManager.getMultipathPreference(Network)
options.verdict: ADOPT AS TELEMETRY ONLY — it is explicitly a hint, not a gate. Read it, log it, optionally soften cellular use when it returns 0; never let it decide whether Bond runs.
options.androidSupport: API 26+, requires ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE. Verbatim javadoc: 'Provides a hint to the calling application on whether it is desirable to use the multinetwork APIs (e.g., Network#openConnection, Network#bindSocket, etc.) for multipath data transfer on this network when it is not the system default network. Applications desiring to use multipath network protocols should call this method before each such operation.' Returns a bitwise OR of MULTIPATH_PREFERENCE_HANDOVER(1), MULTIPATH_PREFERENCE_RELIABILITY(2), MULTIPATH_PREFERENCE_PERFORMANCE(4). It is derived from carrier config + the user's data plan/Data Saver state; it controls NOTHING in the stack and is not enforced. Passing null returns the preference that generally applies to metered networks.

options.name: LTE + 5G as two separate paths on one SIM
options.verdict: REJECT — physically and architecturally impossible. Do not put this on a roadmap slide.
options.androidSupport: None, and none is coming. In 5G NSA/EN-DC the LTE eNB is the master node and the split happens at the PDCP layer INSIDE the RAN; the core delivers a single S1-U bearer and the UE presents ONE IP address / one PDN. There is no second Network object, no second interface, nothing to bind to. Android exposes the radio type only as a read-only display value (TelephonyDisplayInfo / OVERRIDE_NETWORK_TYPE_NR_NSA) — informational, not addressable. Even on 5G SA it is still one PDN unless the carrier provisions a second APN, which consumer SIMs do not.
options.iosSupport: Same constraint — it is a 3GPP architecture fact, not an OS policy.

options.name: Dual-SIM as two simultaneous data paths
options.verdict: REJECT for v1. Blunt version: dual-SIM is two paths only on DSDA hardware, and even there Android gives a normal app no public API to bind a socket to the second subscription's internet network. Treat as unavailable.
options.androidSupport: Hardware-gated and API-gated. DSDS (the overwhelming majority of devices) has one transceiver — only one subscription transmits/receives at a time, so it is one data path by definition. DSDA devices have activeModemCount==2 and CAN carry two data connections, but the internet NetworkRequest is satisfied against the default data subscription; NetworkRequest.Builder#setSubscriptionIds / setNetworkSpecifier(TelephonyNetworkSpecifier) for a non-default subscription is not usable by ordinary apps, and TelephonyManager.getSubscriptionId() only tells you which sub a PhoneAccountHandle maps to (needs READ_PHONE_STATE, a runtime permission). No stock path to two concurrent bindable cellular Networks.
options.iosSupport: Worse — iOS exposes no per-SIM binding at all.
options.natTraversal: Would be two separate carrier NATs if it worked.

options.name: Two Wi-Fi networks at once (STA+STA multi-internet)
options.verdict: REJECT — hard-blocked for third-party apps. The capability exists in AOSP from Android 13 but only privileged/system apps can turn it on.
options.androidSupport: Android 12 added STA/STA concurrency; Android 13 added 'concurrent multiple networks with internet connection'. WifiManager#isStaConcurrencyForMultiInternetSupported() is readable, but AOSP states only privileged apps may call WifiManager#setStaConcurrencyForMultiInternetMode(int) (WIFI_MULTI_INTERNET_MODE_DBS_AP or _MULTI_AP). A Play-distributed APK cannot enable it. So 'Wi-Fi + hotspot Wi-Fi' as two Bond paths is off the table.
options.desktopSupport: Possible on desktop with two adapters — a real desktop-vs-mobile asymmetry worth designing for.

options.name: USB-Ethernet adapter as a third path (TRANSPORT_ETHERNET / TRANSPORT_USB)
options.verdict: PROTOTYPE — real, cheap to support, but niche. Add TRANSPORT_ETHERNET to the path enumerator and let it appear if present; do not build hardware assumptions on it.
options.androidSupport: TransportType constants are stable: Cellular=0, Wifi=1, Bluetooth=2, Ethernet=3, Vpn=4, WifiAware=5, Lowpan=6, Usb=8, Thread=9, Satellite=10. A USB-C-to-Ethernet adapter with in-kernel driver surfaces as a Network with TRANSPORT_ETHERNET and is bindable exactly like the others. TRANSPORT_USB is mostly the upstream marker for USB tethering, not what you want. Adapter driver coverage is OEM-dependent — test, don't assume.
options.iosSupport: iPadOS/iOS supports USB-Ethernet but with no equivalent binding API.
options.natTraversal: Ordinary NAT, same relay correlation as the others.

options.name: MPTCP (Multipath TCP) on Android
options.verdict: REJECT. Android does not expose MPTCP. Every working Android MPTCP demo is a custom kernel on hardware from a decade ago.
options.androidSupport: None usable. Upstream Linux enables MPTCP per-socket via socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, IPPROTO_MPTCP), but Android's bionic/NDK does not expose it, GKI ships it disabled, and there is no ConnectivityService/NetworkAgent integration for adding subflows across Networks. The MPTCP project's own Android page tops out at Nexus 5 / Android 4.4. Even if the kernel cooperated, MPTCP subflow creation would still need per-subflow source binding — i.e. you would be back to bindSocket() anyway.
options.iosSupport: iOS DOES have MPTCP (NSURLSessionMultipathServiceType) — so this is an asymmetry, not a universal no. But it is TCP-only and handover-biased, poorly suited to live video.

options.name: VpnService + setUnderlyingNetworks() (the Speedify model)
options.verdict: PROTOTYPE, DO NOT ADOPT FOR V1. It is proven (Speedify ships it) but it is the right answer only if you want to bond OTHER apps' traffic. For LIVETAP's own encoder output it adds a consent dialog, a persistent VPN key icon, one-VPN-at-a-time exclusivity, and Play policy scrutiny — for zero benefit, since you already control the sockets.
options.androidSupport: VpnService.prepare() requires an explicit user consent Activity; only one active VPN per device. You still need Network.bindSocket() on each tunnel socket, then VpnService.protect() to keep them out of your own tunnel, then setUnderlyingNetworks(Network[]) so the system attributes data correctly. Per javadoc, setUnderlyingNetworks 'only needs to be called if the VPN has explicitly bound its underlying communications channels ... to a Network using APIs such as Network.bindSocket'.
options.iosSupport: NEPacketTunnelProvider equivalent; requires a paid entitlement.

options.name: Foreground service type: camera + microphone (vs dataSync)
options.verdict: ADOPT camera|microphone. REJECT dataSync as the primary type — on Android 15+ it is capped at 6 hours per 24, which would kill a long broadcast mid-stream.
options.androidSupport: FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_CAMERA (manifest FOREGROUND_SERVICE_CAMERA + runtime CAMERA) and FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_MICROPHONE (manifest FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MICROPHONE + runtime RECORD_AUDIO) carry NO time limit — Android's timeout doc says the restriction 'only applies to dataSync and mediaProcessing foreground service type foreground services'. The tradeoff: camera/microphone are subject to while-in-use restrictions — the service CANNOT be started while the app is in the background, and cannot start from BOOT_COMPLETED. So Bond must be started from a visible Studio screen, which matches the product anyway. For screen-share broadcasts use FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_MEDIA_PROJECTION (also untimed, requires createScreenCaptureIntent() consent first).

hardConstraints: NET_CAPABILITY_VALIDATED CANNOT BE REQUESTED. Verbatim javadoc: 'It is presently unsupported to request a network with either NetworkCapabilities#NET_CAPABILITY_VALIDATED or NetworkCapabilities#NET_CAPABILITY_CAPTIVE_PORTAL as these NetworkCapabilities represent states that a particular network may never attain, and whether a network will attain these states is unknown prior to bringing up the network.' Consequence for Bond: you must request on INTERNET only, then WAIT for onCapabilitiesChanged() to report VALIDATED before you trust a path. A path can go onAvailable() and still be a captive-portal hotel Wi-Fi that black-holes your stream. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/android.net.connectivitymanager.requestnetwork?view=net-android-35.0

bindSocket() THROWS ON A CONNECTED SOCKET. All three overloads state flatly: 'The socket must not be connected.' You must create the socket, bind it to the Network, THEN connect. This is the single biggest integration risk in the repo: RootEncoder's RtmpClient creates and connects its own java.net.Socket internally, so you cannot retrofit path binding onto it from outside. Bond must own its own sockets end-to-end (phone -> LIVETAP relay), with RTMP reconstructed relay-side. Design Bond's phone leg as your own protocol over DatagramSocket/DatagramChannel per path, bound before connect. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/android.net.network.bindsocket?view=net-android-35.0

HARD CAP OF 100 OUTSTANDING NETWORK REQUESTS PER UID. Verbatim: 'the system will limit the number of outstanding requests to 100 per app (identified by their UID), shared with all variants of this method, of #registerNetworkCallback as well as ConnectivityDiagnosticsManager#registerConnectivityDiagnosticsCallback. ... If this limit is exceeded, an exception will be thrown.' It is a PER-PROCESS-LIFETIME leak counter, not a concurrency counter — a reconnect loop that re-requests without unregisterNetworkCallback()/releaseNetworkRequest() crashes the app on the 101st attempt. Bond's path supervisor must be idempotent: one long-lived callback object per path, never a new one per retry. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/android.net.connectivitymanager.requestnetwork?view=net-android-35.0

LTE AND 5G ARE NOT TWO PATHS ON ONE SIM. Ever. In 5G NSA/EN-DC the split is at PDCP inside the RAN with the LTE eNB as master node; the core sees one S1-U bearer and the UE holds ONE IP on one PDN. Android has no second Network, no second interface, no binding target. TelephonyDisplayInfo/OVERRIDE_NETWORK_TYPE_NR_NSA is a display string only. Sources: https://www.sharetechnote.com/html/5G/5G_LTE_Interworking.html and https://tech-academy.amarisoft.com/NR_NSA_SplitBearer.html

TWO INTERNET-BEARING WI-FI NETWORKS IS PRIVILEGED-ONLY. AOSP: multi-internet STA/STA exists from Android 13, but 'privileged apps can enable the feature using WifiManager#setStaConcurrencyForMultiInternetMode(int mode)'. A Play-store LIVETAP APK cannot call it. Source: https://source.android.com/docs/core/connect/wifi-sta-sta-concurrency

DUAL-SIM IS NOT TWO PATHS FOR A NORMAL APP. DSDS hardware is single-transceiver (one sub transmits at a time). DSDA hardware can, but binding a socket to the non-default data subscription has no public API route. Assume one cellular path per device.

MPTCP IS NOT AVAILABLE ON ANDROID. No bionic/NDK exposure of IPPROTO_MPTCP, disabled in GKI, no NetworkAgent integration. Last working Android port was Nexus 5 / Android 4.4. Sources: https://multipath-tcp.org/pmwiki.php/Users/Android and https://docs.kernel.org/networking/mptcp.html

dataSync FOREGROUND SERVICE = 6 HOURS PER 24, ANDROID 15+. 'The system permits dataSync and mediaProcessing foreground services to run for a total of 6 hours in a 24-hour period, after which the system calls Service.onTimeout(int, int)'. Then you get seconds to stopSelf() or the system throws, and a restart attempt throws ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException ('Time limit already exhausted for foreground service type dataSync'). If Bond's uploader lives in a dataSync FGS, long streams die. Use camera|microphone (untimed). Source: https://developer.android.com/develop/background-work/services/fgs/timeout

camera / microphone FGS CANNOT BE STARTED FROM THE BACKGROUND (while-in-use restriction), and on Android 15+ cannot be launched from a BOOT_COMPLETED receiver. Bond must be user-initiated from a visible screen. Source: https://developer.android.com/develop/background-work/services/fgs/service-types

DATA SAVER CAN BLOCK THE CELLULAR PATH. Cellular is metered by definition, so it will never carry NET_CAPABILITY_NOT_METERED. When ConnectivityManager.getRestrictBackgroundStatus() returns RESTRICT_BACKGROUND_STATUS_ENABLED, metered background data is blocked outright for the app. Bond must read this and getMultipathPreference() and tell the user why the cellular path is unavailable rather than silently streaming single-path. Source: https://developer.android.com/develop/connectivity/network-ops/data-saver

EVERY BYTE ON THE CELLULAR PATH IS THE USER'S PAID DATA, AND YOU ARE DUPLICATING IT. Bonding with redundancy means a 6 Mbps stream can burn well over 6 Mbps of metered data (~2.7 GB/hour at 6 Mbps before any FEC/duplication overhead). This is a product/consent problem, not a technical one, and it needs an explicit in-app cap and disclosure.

BATTERY: THERE IS NO FREE 'KEEP CELLULAR UP' SWITCH. The only app-accessible mechanism is holding the requestNetwork() open — the cellular radio stays powered for as long as you hold it, and the radio also stays awake 20-30s after each transmission. The 'Mobile data always active' Developer Option does the same thing device-wide but is a USER setting you cannot toggle programmatically. Expect the cellular path alone to be a meaningful drain on top of camera + encoder. Sources: https://developer.android.com/develop/connectivity/preserving-battery and https://developer.android.com/develop/connectivity/minimize-effect-regular-updates

OEM BATTERY MANAGERS OVERRIDE CORRECT CODE. Xiaomi/Huawei autostart gating and Samsung 'deep sleeping' operate below the Android API surface — a correctly-configured, notification-showing foreground service can still be killed. This is a support-burden constraint, not something you can fix in code; plan an in-app 'disable battery optimization' prompt (REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS) and a dontkillmyapp-style help page. Source: https://dontkillmyapp.com/stock_android

THE RELAY CANNOT IDENTIFY PATHS BY IP. Each bound socket exits via a different NAT (home router vs carrier CGNAT), so the relay sees uncorrelated source addresses that can also change mid-stream on cellular. Path identity must be an application-level session+path ID carried in every packet. Plan for CGNAT: carrier paths are outbound-only, so the relay must never try to dial back.

LOCAL NETWORK ACCESS IS BEING GATED BEHIND A NEW RUNTIME PERMISSION (rolling out across the 25Q2 and 26Q2 releases). This does not affect reaching an internet relay, but it WILL affect any LAN discovery feature (finding a desktop LIVETAP instance, a local relay, or an RTMP target on the same subnet). Source: https://developer.android.com/about/versions/16/behavior-changes-all
report.recommendation:
Build Bond's Android leg on exactly one mechanism and stop looking: one long-lived ConnectivityManager.requestNetwork() per path (TRANSPORT_WIFI, TRANSPORT_CELLULAR, and opportunistically TRANSPORT_ETHERNET, each with NET_CAPABILITY_INTERNET and NOT NET_CAPABILITY_VALIDATED), held for the whole broadcast, with Network.bindSocket() applied to a fresh unconnected DatagramSocket per path before connect. Declare CHANGE_NETWORK_STATE and ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE (both normal, both free). Run it inside a foreground service typed camera|microphone — never dataSync — and start it only from a visible Studio screen.

Scope the alpha to TWO paths. That is the honest ceiling on a stock phone: Wi-Fi plus one cellular. Say so in the product copy. Any marketing that implies "LTE + 5G" or "both SIMs" is a claim Android cannot honour, and LIVETAP's stated discipline is not claiming to broadcast when it cannot.

Three engineering decisions follow directly and should be made now, before code:
1. Bond owns its sockets. RootEncoder's RtmpClient connects its own socket internally and bindSocket() refuses connected sockets, so path binding cannot be bolted on. The phone->relay leg must be LIVETAP's own datagram protocol; RTMP is reconstructed relay-side. Treat this as the architectural fork, not an implementation detail.
2. Path readiness is VALIDATED, not onAvailable(). Because VALIDATED is unrequestable, a path is "up" only after onCapabilitiesChanged() reports it. Gate the "Bonded" indicator on that, and surface NOT_SUSPENDED loss and getLinkUpstreamBandwidthKbps() as advisory telemetry only — carrier bandwidth estimates are coarse and must never be your scheduler's primary signal. Measure your own goodput per path.
3. One callback object per path, forever. The 100-request-per-UID lifetime cap turns a naive reconnect loop into a crash. Make the path supervisor idempotent and always release on teardown.

Read getMultipathPreference() and getRestrictBackgroundStatus() at stream start and treat them as user-consent inputs, not gates: if Data Saver is on or the carrier hint is 0, show the user why the cellular path is off and let them override — don't silently downgrade to single-path while the UI still says "Bonded".

Skip VpnService for v1. It is the proven approach (Speedify) but it only earns its consent dialog and its one-VPN-per-device exclusivity if you are bonding other apps' traffic. You aren't.

Verify on real hardware before committing: hold Wi-Fi + cellular for 60 minutes on a Pixel (clean AOSP) and a Samsung (aggressive OEM manager), measuring actual concurrent throughput, battery delta, and whether the FGS survives. That test is cheap and it is the one that decides whether Bond ships.
uncertainties: I could not retrieve the full verbatim javadoc for requestNetwork(NetworkRequest, NetworkCallback) — developer.android.com renders via JS and the AOSP source fetch was truncated. The 100-request limit, the CHANGE_NETWORK_STATE requirement and the VALIDATED prohibition are quoted verbatim from the PendingIntent overload, which the docs state 'behaves identically'. Worth a five-minute confirmation read of the real javadoc before it goes in a design doc.

How long a requested cellular network actually SURVIVES alongside Wi-Fi under real carrier + OEM conditions is not documented anywhere I could source, and AOSP's network-selection page does not state that a third-party app's outstanding request unconditionally prevents teardown. The mechanism is sound and Speedify's shipping product is strong circumstantial evidence, but the duration must be measured on device, not assumed. This is the single most important unknown in the report.

Actual achievable concurrent throughput on Wi-Fi + cellular is unmeasured. Holding two networks is not the same as getting the sum of their bandwidth; thermal limits, modem power budgets and Wi-Fi/LTE coexistence interference on shared antennas can cost real throughput. No vendor publishes this. Measure it.

Battery cost of holding the cellular radio up for a full broadcast is only qualitatively sourced ('radio stays awake 20-30s after each packet', 'keeps pinging cell towers'). I found no quantitative mAh/hour figure for concurrent Wi-Fi + cellular under continuous upload. Needs a bench measurement, ideally alongside the camera+encoder load so the marginal cost of Bond is isolated.

Android 16/17 behavior-change coverage is thinner than I would like — the searches surfaced Android 17 and Android 16 pages but I did not fetch them in full. I found no evidence of any change to requestNetwork/bindSocket semantics in 16 or 17, but I cannot assert the absence of one. Re-check developer.android.com/about/versions/16/behavior-changes-16 and .../17/behavior-changes-17 before locking the design.

USB-Ethernet adapter behaviour (does it reliably produce a bindable TRANSPORT_ETHERNET Network on mainstream phones, or is driver coverage patchy?) is not documented by Google and the sources I found were forum-level. Treat as untested.

Google Play policy risk for an app that holds a cellular network open for hours was not researched. Probably fine given camera/microphone FGS types are the sanctioned pattern for live broadcast, but the foreground-service-type declaration review process has tightened through API 34-36 and deserves its own check.

verdict.claim: That Bond's Android leg should be built on exactly one mechanism — one long-lived ConnectivityManager.requestNetwork() per transport + Network.bindSocket() on an unconnected DatagramSocket — and that because bindSocket() "refuses connected sockets," RootEncoder cannot be retrofitted, so the phone→relay leg MUST be a bespoke LIVETAP datagram protocol with RTMP reconstructed relay-side ("the architectural fork"). Plus the supporting hard constraints: Data Saver can block the cellular path; the 100-request cap is a process-lifetime leak counter; two paths is the honest ceiling; dual-SIM has "no public API route."
verdict.reasoning:
The transport-request skeleton survives. The expensive conclusion drawn from it does not, and four stated "hard constraints" are wrong, overstated, or a platform generation out of date.

R1 — DECISION #1 IS FALSE, AND IT IS THE MOST EXPENSIVE ITEM IN THE PLAN.
(a) Network.getSocketFactory() exists for exactly this. AOSP Network.java returns a NetworkBoundSocketFactory; its sockets are bound to the Network AT CREATION, so "must not be connected" never applies. Android's own guidance prefers it: "Using individually bound Sockets created by Network.getSocketFactory().createSocket() and performing network-specific host name resolutions via Network.getAllByName is preferred to calling bindProcessToNetwork." https://developer.android.com/reference/android/net/Network
(b) "All three overloads state flatly 'The socket must not be connected'" — the javadoc sentence is on all three, but only bindSocket(FileDescriptor) enforces it (explicit Os.getpeername check throwing "Socket is connected"). bindSocket(DatagramSocket) and bindSocket(Socket) contain no isConnected() check; they only touch getReuseAddress() to reach the fd. Source: https://android.googlesource.com/platform/packages/modules/Connectivity/+/refs/heads/main/framework/src/android/net/Network.java
(c) Below Java there is NO check. setNetworkForSocket() in https://android.googlesource.com/platform/system/netd/+/refs/heads/main/client/NetdClient.cpp is `CHECK_SOCKET_IS_MARKABLE(socketFd)` (valid fd, AF_INET/AF_INET6 only) then a SELECT_NETWORK FwmarkCommand — no getpeername. The NDK route android_setsocknetwork() (<android/multinetwork.h>, API 23) says only "Set the network to be used by the given socket file descriptor... This is the equivalent of: android.net.Network::bindSocket()" and says nothing about connected sockets. https://developer.android.com/ndk/reference/group/networking  (Honest caveat: re-marking an ESTABLISHED TCP connection does not migrate it — the 5-tuple and route are fixed at connect. The usable move is mark-then-connect, which both routes allow.)
(d) The library-specific claim is wrong on its own terms. RootEncoder does not scatter `new Socket()` through RtmpClient: it funnels creation through com.pedro.common.socket.base.StreamSocket with createTcpSocket(...) / createUdpSocket(...) and a SocketType enum (JAVA | KTOR) — and createUdpSocket already takes a source-binding parameter. https://github.com/pedroSG94/RootEncoder/tree/master/common/src/main/java/com/pedro/common/socket  It is Apache-2.0, already in the repo, and already ships SRT and UDP clients, not just RTMP. Injecting a network-bound factory is a small patch or an upstream PR.
Net effect: the recommendation turns "add a bound socket factory" into "design, build and maintain a proprietary multipath datagram transport plus a relay that reconstructs RTMP." That is the biggest cost in the document and its stated justification does not hold.

R2 — "DATA SAVER CAN BLOCK THE CELLULAR PATH" does not apply to Bond. Data Saver blocks BACKGROUND metered data: "the system blocks background data usage and signals apps to use less data in the foreground wherever possible." RESTRICT_BACKGROUND_STATUS_ENABLED is defined as "Apps should make an effort to limit data usage in the foreground and gracefully handle restrictions to background data usage" — a request, not a block. https://developer.android.com/develop/connectivity/network-ops/data-saver  NetworkPolicyManagerService carries ALLOWED_REASON_NOT_IN_BACKGROUND / ALLOWED_METERED_REASON_* exemptions. A broadcast user-initiated from a visible Studio screen under a camera|microphone FGS is never in the Data-Saver background bucket. The recommended consent/override UI would tell users a path is off for a reason that isn't operating. Same for getMultipathPreference(): it returns MULTIPATH_PREFERENCE_HANDOVER/RELIABILITY/PERFORMANCE hints for opportunistic multipath — a hint, not policy; "carrier hint is 0" is not a reason to drop a path.

R3 — "PER-PROCESS-LIFETIME leak counter, not a concurrency counter" is unsupported and contradicted by the javadoc they quoted. The text says "outstanding requests," and its own remedy is "make sure to unregister the callbacks with unregisterNetworkCallback()... or releaseNetworkRequest()" — a remedy that only functions if release frees the slot. No AOSP source supports a monotonic counter. The advice (idempotent supervisor, always release) is right; the mechanism claim is invented, and a team that believes it will build a pointless process-restart escape hatch.

R4 — THE ANALYSIS IS A PLATFORM GENERATION STALE. It is 2026 and Android 17 (API 37) is shipping; it is never mentioned. Android 17 background audio hardening applies REGARDLESS of targetSdk: "All apps running on Android 17 that have these background audio interactions must have a visible activity or must be running a foreground service that is not of type SHORT_SERVICE." Apps targeting API 37 additionally need a while-in-use FGS; audio focus fails AUDIOFOCUS_REQUEST_FAILED and playback/volume APIs "fail silently without throwing." https://developer.android.com/about/versions/17/changes/bg-audio  Local network: the permission is ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK, opt-in on Android 16 and MANDATORY for apps targeting API 37 — https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/local-network-permission — and Play has required targetSdk 36 since 31 Aug 2026, so "rolling out across 25Q2 and 26Q2" understates a dated obligation. (Their FGS-timeout point does survive: the timeout page, last updated 2026-09-01, still limits 6h/24h to dataSync, mediaProcessing and shortService — camera/microphone remain untimed. https://developer.android.com/develop/background-work/services/fgs/timeout)

R5 — "TWO paths is the honest ceiling" contradicts their own recommendation, which requests TRANSPORT_ETHERNET opportunistically. USB-C Ethernet and Bluetooth PAN each surface as a distinct Network with NET_CAPABILITY_INTERNET. The defensible sentence is "at most one cellular path," not "two paths."

R6 — SOURCING. Every Android API citation is learn.microsoft.com .NET-for-Android binding docs (auto-generated mirrors, ms.date 2024-05-01), not developer.android.com or AOSP. That mirror is precisely what hid getSocketFactory() and the fact that only one overload enforces the connected rule. The MPTCP citation, multipath-tcp.org/.../Users/Android, documents the ABANDONED out-of-tree MPTCP v0.9x port (Nexus 5 / KitKat) — a different codebase from upstream in-kernel MPTCP (Linux 5.6+). The conclusion is right for the wrong reason; the real evidence is that CONFIG_MPTCP is ABSENT from the Android GKI arch/arm64/configs/gki_defconfig (android15-6.6) and IPPROTO_MPTCP is absent from bionic's netinet/in.h. Cite those.

R7 — "Binding to the non-default data subscription has no public API route" is literally false. android.net.TelephonyNetworkSpecifier is public API since API 30 (Builder.setSubscriptionId), and NetworkRequest.Builder.setSubscriptionIds(Set<Integer>) is public since API 35. The actual gate is in that javadoc: "Registering a request with a non-empty subscription-ID set requires the NETWORK_FACTORY permission" — signature-level, unavailable to a Play app. Same ceiling, correct reason; "no API exists" sends an engineer looking, "signature-gated" closes it.

R8 — MISSED SHIPPING CONSTRAINT. Targeting Android 14+, every declared FGS type must be declared on the Play Console App content page, "required to include a link to a video demonstrating each foreground service feature." Picking camera|microphone because it is untimed is a Play-review surface decision, not only a technical one. https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/13392821

R9 — THE ALTERNATIVE THEY NEVER EVALUATED. SRT connection bonding shipped in libsrt 1.5 socket groups (broadcast / main-backup / balancing) and RootEncoder already has an SRT client. Report it honestly: Haivision's own docs mark balancing "UNDER DEVELOPMENT," and SRT binds group members by SOURCE ADDRESS, which is insufficient on Android — routing is fwmark-based, so a source-IP bind without the netid mark falls to the default table; you would still need android_setsocknetwork() per member UDP fd. Candidate, not freebie. https://github.com/Haivision/srt/blob/master/docs/features/socket-groups.md  And multipath QUIC is still an Internet-Draft (draft-ietf-quic-multipath, now at -21, no RFC number) — not a shipped standard.

WHAT SURVIVES: requestNetwork-per-transport with long-lived callbacks; camera|microphone over dataSync; VALIDATED being unrequestable (so gate on onCapabilitiesChanged); one cellular path per device; MPTCP unavailable on Android; STA/STA multi-internet privileged-only; CGNAT means app-level session+path IDs and outbound-only; the metered-data cost disclosure; OEM battery killers; and the 60-minute Pixel+Samsung hardware test, which is still the right next action.
verdict.correction: Keep the transport skeleton; kill the architectural fork. (1) You do NOT need a bespoke datagram protocol to get per-path binding. Use Network.getSocketFactory() — sockets are bound at creation, so the "must not be connected" rule is never reached — or android_setsocknetwork() on the fd before connect in native code. Only bindSocket(FileDescriptor) actually enforces the connected check; netd's setNetworkForSocket() does not check at all. RootEncoder already routes all socket creation through StreamSocket.createTcpSocket/createUdpSocket with a SocketType enum, so per-path binding is a small patch to an Apache-2.0 dependency you already ship, not a rewrite. Decide the phone→relay protocol on multipath-scheduling merits (SRT socket groups vs. your own), not on a binding constraint that does not exist. (2) Data Saver does not block a foreground broadcast — it blocks background metered data. Keep the data-cost disclosure and the in-app cap; delete the getRestrictBackgroundStatus()/getMultipathPreference() gate and its override UI, or you will show users a blocker that is not blocking them. (3) The 100-request cap is an outstanding-request (concurrency) counter — the javadoc's own remedy is to unregister. Idempotent supervisor is still right; drop the "lifetime leak" framing. (4) Redo the platform pass against Android 17 / API 37, not Android 15: background-audio hardening applies regardless of targetSdk, ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK is mandatory at API 37, and Play has required targetSdk 36 since 31 Aug 2026. (5) Say "at most one cellular path," not "two paths total" — Ethernet and Bluetooth PAN are real third paths and your own recommendation already requests Ethernet. (6) Re-cite everything from developer.android.com / AOSP rather than the learn.microsoft.com binding mirror; for MPTCP cite the absent CONFIG_MPTCP in GKI gki_defconfig and absent IPPROTO_MPTCP in bionic, not the dead out-of-tree Nexus 5 page. (7) Dual-SIM: the API exists (TelephonyNetworkSpecifier, API 30; NetworkRequest.Builder.setSubscriptionIds, API 35) and is gated by the signature-level NETWORK_FACTORY permission. (8) Budget for the Play Console FGS declaration and its required demo video before choosing camera|microphone.

report.summary: Apple's MPTCP stack is the wrong tool for LIVETAP Bond, and Apple's own documentation says so explicitly: `.aggregate` — the only mode that actually stripes one connection across Wi-Fi and cellular — is documented as "available only for experimentation" and requires an iPhone in Developer mode with Settings > Developer > Multipath Networking turned on. It cannot ship. `.handover` and `.interactive` are failover/latency modes, not bandwidth aggregation, and all three additionally require the destination server to speak MPTCP, which Apple platforms themselves cannot do (client-side only, client-initiated subflows only). The good news is that the entitlement question is moot and the actual path is proven: Moblin, an MIT-licensed iOS app shipping on the App Store, bonds one cellular + one Wi-Fi + multiple Ethernet paths using plain per-interface UDP `NWConnection`s with `NWParameters.requiredInterface`, and carries zero networking entitlements to do it. That is the pattern LIVETAP Bond should reserve for Apple.
report.recommendation:
**Build app-level multipath over UDP. Do not build on MPTCP. Do not build a VPN.**

The reference implementation already exists and is MIT-licensed: Moblin (github.com/eerimoq/moblin, App Store id6466745933). The exact recipe, from `Moblin/Media/Srtla/Client/RemoteConnection.swift`:

```swift
let params = NWParameters(dtls: .none)   // plain UDP
params.prohibitExpensivePaths = false    // MUST be false or cellular is excluded
params.requiredInterface = interface     // a concrete NWInterface, not a type
connection = NWConnection(host: h, port: p, using: params)
```

Paths are discovered in `SrtlaClient.handleNetworkPathUpdate(path:)` by walking `path.availableInterfaces` filtered to `[.cellular, .wifi, .wiredEthernet]`, creating one `RemoteConnection` per `NWInterface`, and tearing down connections whose interface disappears from the path. Moblin's `Moblin.all.entitlements` contains **no** multipath, multicast, or NetworkExtension entitlement — this is all unprivileged API.

**What the LIVETAP Bond abstraction must reserve for Apple:**

1. **A path handle that is an opaque platform object, not a string.** Android gives you a `Network` object you bind a socket to; Apple gives you an `NWInterface` you assign to `NWParameters.requiredInterface`. Neither is a stable interface name (`NWInterface` has no public initializer — you can only obtain instances from a live `NWPath`). Do not model paths as `"wlan0"` / `"en0"`. Model them as `{ opaque handle, enum kind, display name, cost class }`.

2. **The transport must be UDP-based, not TCP-based.** MPTCP is off the table, so the relay protocol must be SRTLA, RIST, or a LIVETAP-native UDP protocol. This is not an iOS-only consequence — it is also what lets you do per-packet scheduling, which MPTCP's aggregate mode would not have given you portably anyway.

3. **The relay must be the connection initiator's peer, never the subflow initiator.** Apple's MPTCP supports only client-initiated subflows, and more importantly every app-level path is an outbound UDP flow from the device. Design the relay to accept N independent UDP flows that self-identify with a group/session ID (SRTLA's `REG1`/`REG2` handshake model — Moblin's `register(groupId:)`). The relay must never need to dial back to the device. This makes NAT traversal a non-issue on all platforms.

4. **Reserve a per-path "expensive/constrained" flag in the scheduler.** On Apple this maps to `NWPath.isExpensive` / `isConstrained`; you must set `prohibitExpensivePaths = false` to use cellular at all, and Apple's guidance is to honour `prohibitConstrainedPaths` so Low Data Mode still means something. Ship a user-visible per-path priority/enable control (Moblin has one) so the user, not the OS, decides when to burn cellular data.

5. **Reserve a lifecycle hook for "the OS is about to suspend us."** iOS tears down network connections when a process suspends. LIVETAP iOS will need `UIBackgroundModes` containing `audio` and an active `AVAudioSession` to survive backgrounding — that is how Moblin does it. Budget for this; it is an iOS-specific requirement with no Android analogue.

6. **Do not reserve anything for MPTCP.** If you ever want MPTCP, it is a one-line `params.multipathServiceType = .handover` on a TCP connection and requires a Linux relay with kernel ≥5.6 listening on an `IPPROTO_MPTCP` socket. Treat it as a possible future *reliability* feature for the control channel, never as the bonding mechanism.

**Account/entitlement work required before iOS ships: none for Bond itself.** A paid Apple Developer Program membership is needed (free Personal Team provisioning does not include restricted capabilities), but there is no request form, no approval queue, and no review-time justification for per-interface UDP. This is the single biggest de-risking fact in this report — the Apple networking work for LIVETAP Bond is ordinary application code.

**Sequencing advice:** because the iOS mechanism (per-interface socket + app-level scheduler) is architecturally identical to the Android mechanism (`Network.bindSocket` + the same scheduler), build the scheduler and the relay-side reassembly as platform-agnostic core now, with the platform layer reduced to "enumerate paths, hand me a bound socket." Then iOS is a port of ~300 lines, not a redesign.
hardConstraints: MPTCP `.aggregate` CANNOT SHIP ON iOS. Apple's own docs for `URLSessionConfiguration.MultipathServiceType.aggregate`: "This option is available only for experimentation... To enable the aggregation mode, open the Settings app on your development iPhone and navigate to Developer, and then turn on Multipath Networking. Multipath Aggregation requires an iOS device in Developer mode with a cellular connection running iOS 11.0 or later." A shipped app on a customer's non-developer device gets no striping. This single fact eliminates MPTCP as LIVETAP Bond's transport. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/nsurlsessionmultipathservicetype/nsurlsessionmultipathservicetypeaggregate

On macOS, MPTCP aggregation is off at the kernel level by default: `net.inet.mptcp.allow_aggregate` defaults to 0 (it "controls whether Multipath TCP can actively use two different subflows to send data"). You cannot sysctl a customer's Mac, so `.aggregate` is equally unshippable on desktop. https://mptcp-apps.github.io/mptcp-doc/mptcp-apple.html

MPTCP requires the SERVER to speak MPTCP. Apple, verbatim: "Multipath TCP requires the destination server to have Multipath TCP enabled." A LIVETAP relay would need Linux kernel ≥5.6 (realistically ≥6.1) with an `IPPROTO_MPTCP` listening socket, or an mptcpize-wrapped binary. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/improving-network-reliability-using-multipath-tcp

Apple platforms are MPTCP CLIENT-ONLY. There is no MPTCP `NWListener` on macOS or iOS. A LIVETAP relay can never run on macOS. Apple's implementation also only supports client-initiated subflows, so the relay could never add a path. https://www.mptcp.dev/macOS.html and https://mptcp-apps.github.io/mptcp-doc/mptcp-apple.html

MPTCP fails silently to plain TCP when any middlebox strips TCP option 30. Apple: "If any middleboxes, such as routers or switches, between the iOS device and server don't support MPTCP, iOS makes a standard TCP connection." You would ship a bonding feature that degrades to single-path with no error surface. https://support.apple.com/en-us/101905

Wi-Fi Assist throttles MPTCP on iOS in two ways Apple documents: it "prevents flows from using cellular data when your app is in the background," and it "limits the amount of data that your app can send over cellular networks. When the limit is reached, Multipath TCP is disabled." The override for the data cap exists only in the Developer settings section, i.e. not for customers. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/improving-network-reliability-using-multipath-tcp

The `com.apple.developer.networking.multipath` entitlement does not exist on macOS. Apple's entitlement page lists availability as iOS 3.0+, iPadOS 3.0+, visionOS 1.0+ only, and "Multipath" is absent from the macOS supported-capabilities table (which lists only Custom Network Protocol, Network Extensions, Personal VPN, VMNet as networking capabilities). https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/entitlements/com.apple.developer.networking.multipath and https://developer.apple.com/help/account/reference/supported-capabilities-macos

`URLSession` has NO interface-selection API on any Apple platform — no `requiredInterface`, no `requiredInterfaceType`. `allowsCellularAccess` can only forbid cellular, never require it. Per Apple DTS (Quinn): "You can set allowsCellularAccess to force the connection to avoid WWAN, but there's no opposite setting." Any multipath work must go through Network.framework `NWConnection`. Additionally, `multipathServiceType` cannot be set on `URLSessionConfiguration` on macOS at all. https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/660216 and https://www.mptcp.dev/macOS.html

`NWInterface` has no public initializer. You cannot construct a path handle from an interface name like "en0" or "pdp_ip0"; instances are obtainable only from a live `NWPath` (via `NWPathMonitor`). Any cross-platform path abstraction must therefore carry an opaque platform handle, not a string.

Setting `multipathServiceType` breaks peer-to-peer `NWConnection` establishment on iOS 17.1/17.2/17.4 with both `.handover` and `.interactive`, reproducible with Apple's own TicTacToe sample. Filed FB13401552 (April 2024), still unresolved as of January 2025. Apple DTS's advice was "disabling MPTCP is an easy workaround." https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/750541

App Store Review Guideline 5.4: "Apps offering VPN services must utilize the NEVPNManager API and may only be offered by developers enrolled as an organization." If LIVETAP ever considered the Speedify-style system-wide bonding VPN, an individual developer account cannot ship it, and VPN apps carry extra data-handling commitments and per-territory VPN licensing disclosure. This is a reason to keep bonding inside the app, not in a tunnel.

iOS suspends backgrounded processes and network connections tear or go unresponsive when that happens. Sustained background broadcasting requires an explicit background mode; Moblin declares `UIBackgroundModes` = audio, location, bluetooth-central, voip and relies on an active audio session. There is no generic "keep streaming in background" mode.

`com.apple.developer.avfoundation.multitasking-camera-access` — often reached for by camera-streaming apps — was deprecated in iOS 18.0; Apple says to use `AVCaptureSession.isMultitaskingCameraAccessSupported` instead. It was also historically restricted to apps declaring `voip` in UIBackgroundModes. Do not design around it. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/entitlements/com.apple.developer.avfoundation.multitasking-camera-access
