Multipath QUIC (draft-ietf-quic-multipath) is NOT exposed by Network.framework. Apple's QUIC support (`NWProtocolQUIC`, and the iOS 26 `NetworkConnection`/`NetworkListener` APIs) offers no multipath surface. There is no Apple API for striping a QUIC connection across interfaces.

options.name: App-level multipath over UDP with NWParameters.requiredInterface (SRTLA / RIST / LIVETAP-native)
options.verdict: ADOPT. This is the only Apple-shippable way to stripe one live broadcast across Wi-Fi + cellular + Ethernet. Proven in a shipping App Store app, needs zero entitlements, and is architecturally identical to the Android approach so the scheduler is shared code.
options.iosSupport: Full. iOS 12.0+. One `NWConnection` per `NWInterface` from `NWPathMonitor`'s `path.availableInterfaces`, with `NWParameters(dtls: .none)`, `params.requiredInterface = interface`, `params.prohibitExpensivePaths = false`. Moblin ships exactly this on the App Store (id6466745933) bonding one cellular + one Wi-Fi + multiple Ethernet.
options.androidSupport: Equivalent mechanism exists (ConnectivityManager.requestNetwork + Network.bindSocket). Out of this lens's scope but confirms the abstraction ports.
options.desktopSupport: macOS 10.14+. Same `requiredInterface` API, same availability dates (iOS/iPadOS/Mac Catalyst 12.0+, macOS 10.14+, tvOS 12.0+, watchOS 5.0+, visionOS 1.0+). macOS keeps Ethernet and Wi-Fi services up concurrently; binding per-interface sidesteps the fact that only one service holds the default route.
options.natTraversal: Trivial and this is the key advantage. Every path is an outbound UDP flow from the device to the relay's fixed public IP:port. The relay never dials back. Paths self-identify with a group/session ID at the relay (SRTLA's REG1/REG2; Moblin's `register(groupId:)`). No STUN, no TURN, no ICE, no hole-punching.
options.license: Moblin is MIT — directly readable and borrowable. SRT/SRTLA reference implementations are MPL-2.0 (libsrt) / MIT (srtla). The Apple APIs used are plain public SDK.

options.name: MPTCP via NWParameters.multipathServiceType = .aggregate
options.maturity: experimental (Apple's own word: "available only for experimentation")
options.verdict: REJECT outright. It is the only mode that would actually stripe bandwidth, and Apple gates it behind a Developer-mode device toggle that no customer has. Building on it means the feature works on your test phone and silently does nothing for every user.
options.iosSupport: API present since iOS 12.0 but non-functional in production. Requires Settings > Developer > Multipath Networking on a Developer-mode device, plus the multipath entitlement, plus a cellular connection, plus iOS 11.0+. Apple also warns it "will use a considerable amount of cellular data."
options.androidSupport: N/A — Android has no MPTCP client API surface; this is an Apple-only construct.
options.desktopSupport: macOS 10.14+ API-wise, but `net.inet.mptcp.allow_aggregate` defaults to 0, so no striping without a sysctl on the user's machine.
options.natTraversal: Poor. Subflows are TCP, client-initiated only, and any middlebox stripping TCP option 30 silently degrades the whole connection to single-path TCP with no error.

options.name: MPTCP .handover
options.verdict: REJECT as a bonding mechanism; consider ONLY as reliability for a non-media TCP control channel. Apple documents it as "Enable multipath, but only use other interfaces when the primary interface is lost" — that is failover, not aggregation. It cannot increase upload bandwidth, which is the entire point of LIVETAP Bond.
options.iosSupport: iOS 12.0+ (Network.framework) / iOS 11.0+ (URLSession). Requires the `com.apple.developer.networking.multipath` entitlement. Apple recommends it as "the best option" for the ordinary seamless-transition use case.
options.androidSupport: N/A for this API. Linux/Android kernels can do MPTCP but there is no equivalent app-facing Android API.
options.desktopSupport: macOS 10.14+ via Network.framework only (URLSession on macOS cannot set multipathServiceType). No entitlement needed on macOS — the capability does not exist there.
options.natTraversal: Same TCP option 30 middlebox fragility; silent fallback to plain TCP.

options.name: MPTCP .interactive
options.verdict: REJECT. Apple: "Enable multipath to use other interfaces when the primary interface encounters loss or delay." It is a latency-hedging mode (this is what Siri uses), not throughput aggregation. Wrong objective function for a sustained high-bitrate upload.
options.iosSupport: iOS 12.0+, entitlement required. Also one of the two modes implicated in the iOS 17.x peer-to-peer NWConnection regression (FB13401552).
options.androidSupport: N/A.

options.name: com.apple.developer.networking.multipath entitlement (the approval question)
options.verdict: NOT A BLOCKER — and also not needed, since the recommended design uses no entitlement at all. Contrary to the usual assumption, this is a self-serve Xcode capability, NOT an approval-gated one. But it only unlocks MPTCP modes that are individually rejected above, so it buys nothing.
options.iosSupport: Apple's instruction is simply "To add this entitlement to your app, enable the Multipath capability in Xcode." No request form exists. Contrast the multicast entitlement, whose docs say verbatim: "This entitlement requires permission from Apple before you can use it in your app. Request permission from the Multicast Networking Entitlement Request page." Multipath has no such sentence and no such page. It does require a paid membership — Apple DTS (Quinn) confirms free Personal Team provisioning supports only a limited capability set that excludes it.
options.androidSupport: N/A.
options.desktopSupport: Does not exist on macOS. Entitlement availability is iOS 3.0+/iPadOS 3.0+/visionOS 1.0+ only, and "Multipath" is not in the macOS supported-capabilities table.

options.name: NEPacketTunnelProvider bonding VPN (the Speedify model)
options.maturity: production (Speedify ships on the App Store, id999025824)
options.verdict: REJECT for LIVETAP. It works and it is approvable, but it drags in App Store Guideline 5.4: VPN apps "may only be offered by developers enrolled as an organization," plus privacy-policy commitments and per-territory VPN licensing disclosure — all to solve a problem you do not have. LIVETAP controls both endpoints of its own stream; it does not need to bond the whole device's traffic.
options.iosSupport: Works. `com.apple.developer.networking.networkextension` with packet-tunnel-provider has been self-serve (no request form) since November 2016 — only Hotspot Helper and the NE app-push provider remain approval-gated. But the 5.4 organization-enrollment rule is the real gate.
options.androidSupport: VpnService equivalent exists; same "why would we" objection.
options.desktopSupport: macOS system extension variant exists (packet-tunnel-provider-systemextension), adds notarization and user-approval friction.
options.natTraversal: Same as app-level UDP — outbound flows to a fixed relay. No advantage over the recommended option.
options.license: Speedify is closed-source; you would be reimplementing, not reusing.

options.name: Multipath QUIC (draft-ietf-quic-multipath)
options.verdict: REJECT for any near-term Apple target. The IETF draft is progressing (draft-ietf-quic-multipath-21) but Apple exposes no multipath surface on `NWProtocolQUIC`, and the iOS 26 `NetworkConnection`/`NetworkListener` rework did not add one. There is no API to call.
options.iosSupport: None. Apple's QUIC has no multipath API. Note also that in the iOS 26 APIs, `NetworkListener.run` requires `OneToOneProtocol` while QUIC conforms to `MultiplexProtocol`, so even ordinary QUIC listener support is still settling.
options.androidSupport: No platform API either; would require bundling a userspace QUIC stack.
options.natTraversal: Would be good in principle (UDP, connection migration), but irrelevant without an implementation.
options.license: Would require a third-party userspace stack; adds a large maintenance surface for no capability the UDP option lacks.

options.name: macOS: Ethernet + Wi-Fi simultaneously via Network.framework
options.verdict: ADOPT for the desktop app — same code as iOS. This is genuinely easier than iOS: no entitlement exists or is needed, no Wi-Fi Assist data cap, no background-suspension problem, and desktop users are the ones most likely to have Ethernet + Wi-Fi + a tethered phone at once.
options.iosSupport: N/A (this row is the macOS lens).
options.androidSupport: N/A.
options.desktopSupport: `NWParameters.requiredInterface` / `requiredInterfaceType` / `prohibitedInterfaceTypes` are all macOS 10.14+. macOS keeps every configured network service up simultaneously; only the default route follows the Network preferences service order, and binding per-interface bypasses that entirely. Moblin's `SrtlaClient` already enumerates `.wiredEthernet` alongside `.wifi` and `.cellular` from the same `NWPathMonitor` code path, so the desktop case is literally the same loop.
options.natTraversal: Same outbound-UDP-to-relay model. No inbound reachability needed.

uncertainties: Whether a free Apple Developer (Personal Team) account can enable the Multipath capability. Apple DTS's forum answer implies not ("there's only a limited set of capabilities you can use" with free provisioning), while the supported-capabilities table appeared to mark it available across membership tiers. Low impact — the recommended design needs no entitlement, and LIVETAP will need a paid ADP membership for App Store distribution regardless.

Apple's App Review has no published guideline specifically about apps using cellular and Wi-Fi simultaneously, and I found no documented rejections for it. The evidence is by existence proof (Moblin and Speedify both ship) rather than by an affirmative Apple statement. Residual risk: an app that burns large volumes of cellular data without clear user control could plausibly attract 2.4.2 (resource usage) or metadata scrutiny. Mitigate by shipping per-path enable/priority toggles and live per-path data counters, as Moblin does.

Moblin declares `voip` in UIBackgroundModes. Since iOS 13, the `voip` background mode is tied to PushKit + CallKit reporting obligations, and declaring it without genuine VoIP behaviour has historically drawn review attention. I could not confirm whether Moblin's use is currently uncontested or merely un-noticed. LIVETAP should plan on `audio` (with a real AVAudioSession) as the background-survival mechanism and treat `voip` as a review risk to avoid.

I did not find an Apple statement on how many concurrent per-interface NWConnections are supported, or whether iOS applies any undocumented throttle to cellular when Wi-Fi is the default route and the app is foregrounded. Moblin's shipping behaviour suggests no practical limit at the 2-4 path scale, but this should be measured on device before committing to a path-count ceiling in the protocol design.

Apple DTS (Quinn) noted a nuance about Wi-Fi networks joined automatically versus manually: "If it was an auto join, iOS will shortly thereafter leave the network... If it was a manual join, iOS will stay on the network but leave the default route set to WWAN." That discussion was in the context of Wi-Fi networks without internet access (accessory networks), and I could not confirm whether any equivalent behaviour affects ordinary internet-bearing Wi-Fi. Worth a device test if LIVETAP ever bonds over a captive/accessory Wi-Fi link. https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/660216

Whether the iOS 17.x regression where `multipathServiceType` breaks peer-to-peer NWConnection (FB13401552) was ever fixed in iOS 18/26/27. It was still open as of the last report I found (January 2025). This only matters if LIVETAP later adds MPTCP to a control channel.

verdict.claim: "Build app-level multipath over UDP, not MPTCP, not a VPN — the reference implementation already exists and is MIT-licensed (Moblin), no Apple entitlement work is required, and iOS is a ~300-line port of the Android mechanism."
verdict.reasoning:
The DIRECTION survives — I could not break the MPTCP or VPN constraints. Every MPTCP claim I spot-checked held, and Multipath QUIC really is still a draft (draft-ietf-quic-multipath-21, March 2026, still not an RFC — https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-quic-multipath-21). App-level per-interface UDP is right.

But three load-bearing de-risking claims are materially false, and each one is a build-stopper the report does not mention.

1. THE MIT REFERENCE IMPLEMENTATION IS ONLY THE SENDER. THE RELAY IS AGPL-3.0 AND ABANDONED BY ITS AUTHOR.
Moblin is MIT (github.com/eerimoq/moblin) — that is the client. The relay, which is the piece LIVETAP must own and run and which the whole architecture depends on, has exactly one reference implementation: `srtla_rec` in https://github.com/BELABOX/srtla, licensed **AGPL-3.0** (https://github.com/BELABOX/srtla/blob/main/LICENSE). Its own README says verbatim: "The server component - srtla_rec - in this repository is unsupported, no longer under development and not suitable for production deployment." AGPL §13 network copyleft is triggered by exactly this deployment shape — a modified AGPL program offered to users over a network obliges you to offer Corresponding Source to every one of those users. The report's central de-risking sentence covers the easy half of the system and is silent on the hard half.

2. SRTLA IS NOT A SPECIFICATION, AND IT NEEDS A FORKED SRT STACK.
No RFC, no VSF TR, no published document. The normative definition of SRTLA is the AGPL C source. Clean-rooming a relay from AGPL source your engineers have read is the weakest possible clean-room posture. Worse, SRTLA does not run on stock libsrt: BELABOX maintains https://github.com/BELABOX/srt, a fork of Haivision/srt described as "SRT tweaked for use with srtla." So the relay needs a patched fork of an MPL-2.0 library plus a clean-room of an AGPL protocol with no spec.
The report listed RIST as an alternative and then reasoned entirely down the SRTLA path without weighing license or spec status — which is the exact criterion the brief said should decide. RIST inverts every one of these: bonding is a first-class feature of **VSF TR-06-2 Main Profile** (a published spec), and libRIST is "released under a very liberal license... so that it can be embedded anywhere, including non-open-source software" (https://github.com/deepin-community/librist/blob/master/README.md), supporting "all features from the TR-06-1 and most of the features of TR-06-2." Caveat found, not hidden: libRIST's multipath is incomplete — https://code.videolan.org/rist/librist/-/issues/47 "Tunnel-Level Multi-Path Operation" is open.

3. "PLATFORM LAYER REDUCED TO 'HAND ME A BOUND SOCKET'" BREAKS ON THE PLATFORM LIVETAP ALREADY SHIPS.
LIVETAP's working product is an Electron desktop app. **Node.js cannot bind a UDP socket to an interface.** `dgram.bind()` takes an address, not an interface, and binding a source IP does not constrain egress — the kernel routes by destination. The real mechanisms are `SO_BINDTODEVICE` (Linux; device-name form is privileged) and `IP_BOUND_IF` (macOS — https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/744044), neither exposed by Node. nodejs/node issue #35769 requested precisely this, describing the Bond use case verbatim — "connect to the same remote address on the same port with two different IP through two different interface" — and it is **closed as not planned** (https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/35769). Desktop Bond therefore requires a native N-API addon per OS. That is not a footnote to a "~300 lines" estimate; it is an unscoped native-code workstream on the one platform that already broadcasts.

4. "NO ENTITLEMENT WORK, NO REVIEW-TIME JUSTIFICATION" IS TRUE FOR BOND AND FALSE FOR THE PRODUCT.
Per-interface UDP needs no entitlement — correct. But to keep the **camera** running while backgrounded on iPhone, `AVCaptureSession.isMultitaskingCameraAccessSupported` must be true, and it is **false on iPhone** (iPad/Stage Manager only). In apps linked against iOS 18+ it becomes true only for apps declaring **`voip`** in `UIBackgroundModes`, or for apps holding `com.apple.developer.avfoundation.multitasking-camera-access`, **which must be requested from Apple** (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/avfoundation/avcapturesession/ismultitaskingcameraaccesssupported). Against App Store Guideline 2.5.4, quoted verbatim from the current guidelines: "Multitasking apps may only use background services for their intended purposes: VoIP, audio playback, location, task completion, local notifications, etc." Declaring `voip` in a broadcast app to unlock background camera IS a review-time justification — the thing the report says does not exist. The report spotted the deprecated entitlement, said "do not design around it," and never stated the consequence: **backgrounded LIVETAP on iPhone keeps audio flowing and stops sending video.** That is a product decision, not an implementation detail, and it is invisible in the report.
verdict.correction:
Keep the direction, discard the risk assessment and re-run the transport choice.

WHAT STANDS: app-level multipath over UDP; no MPTCP; no VPN; relay as pure receiver of N self-identifying outbound flows (NAT traversal genuinely becomes a non-issue); opaque per-path handles rather than interface-name strings; the expensive/constrained flag; the concrete-`NWInterface` mechanism on Apple. All correct, none refuted.

WHAT MUST CHANGE:

1. Re-open the transport decision as a license-and-spec decision, which is how the brief framed it. SRTLA = AGPL-3.0 relay, author-declared unfit for production, no written spec, requires a forked SRT. RIST = published VSF TR-06-1/TR-06-2 spec, permissively-licensed libRIST, bonding is a named profile feature, but libRIST multipath is incomplete (open issue #47). A LIVETAP-native UDP protocol is now a serious third option rather than a luxury, because you are writing a relay from scratch either way. Decide this before writing the scheduler — the relay is the part with no free reference implementation.

2. Never link `srtla_rec` into the LIVETAP relay, and do not let an engineer who has read that source write the relay. If you keep SRTLA-on-the-wire for Moblin/BELABOX interop, treat wire compatibility and implementation as separate decisions.

3. Budget a native addon workstream for Electron desktop: `SO_BINDTODEVICE`/`IP_BOUND_IF` via N-API, per OS. Node will not do this for you and has formally declined to. This is the largest unscoped item in the report.

4. Decide now what backgrounded iPhone does. There is no unprivileged background camera on iPhone. Options: accept audio-only-with-frozen-video when backgrounded and design the UI to say so; or pursue `voip` UIBackgroundModes and prepare a 2.5.4 justification; or request the restricted entitlement from Apple and treat it as a gated dependency with a queue. The report's "no approval queue" claim is only true if you accept option one.

5. Keep the sequencing advice — platform-agnostic scheduler plus thin per-platform path layer is still right. Just size the "thin" layer honestly: unprivileged on iOS and Android, native code on desktop.

One thing I checked and could not break, so do not re-litigate it: the concrete-`NWInterface` approach. The widely-cited "forcing cellular doesn't work" complaints are about `requiredInterfaceType` (the type-based property), not `requiredInterface`. The report already drew that distinction correctly.

report.summary: Multi-path bonding for live video is solved and shipping, and the reference design is public: BELABOX's SRTLA — a thin UDP link-aggregation shim under SRT, sender picks a link per packet by `window / (in_flight_pkts + 1)`, receiver reassembles into one SRT session. It is proven on phones today (Moblin on iOS, Brix and IRL Pro on Android), so LIVETAP Bond is feasible. The two things that will actually decide your design are not protocol choices: (1) a phone has exactly ONE cellular data path — iOS has no DSDA at all, so "Wi-Fi + 5G + LTE from one handset" is not a product you can ship; (2) the relay is a stateful single-public-UDP-port server with heavy egress, which cannot live on Vercel or sanely on hyperscaler egress pricing — the market clearing price for this is ~$10/month/streamer on unmetered bare metal. NAT traversal is a non-problem (all paths are client-initiated outbound UDP to one public host); the real equivalent problem is per-path identity, which SRTLA solves with an in-band 256-byte group ID and, notably, zero authentication.

options.name: SRTLA v2 (BELABOX/srtla) — the protocol
options.license: AGPL-3.0 (code). The wire protocol itself is published, not licensed.
options.natTraversal: Not needed. Every path is an outbound UDP flow to one public ip:port. Receiver never initiates. Works behind CGNAT.
options.iosSupport: Protocol yes (Moblin ships it). This C code, no — Linux only.
options.androidSupport: Protocol yes (Brix, IRL Pro ship it). This C code, no.
options.desktopSupport: Linux only for srtla_send; srtla_rec 'confirmed to work on Windows via WSL1' only.
options.verdict: adopt the protocol, reject the code — AGPL-3.0 poisons both a proprietary mobile binary and, via §13's network clause, a relay you operate as a service.

options.name: srtla_send (C) — sender internals worth copying
options.androidSupport: no
options.desktopSupport: Linux; requires OS-level source routing because it uses bind() to pin a UDP socket to a link
options.verdict: adopt the algorithm. It is ~200 lines of idea: per-link congestion window WINDOW_MIN 1 / WINDOW_DEF 20 / WINDOW_MAX 60, WINDOW_MULT 1000, WINDOW_INCR 30 on ACK, WINDOW_DECR 100 on NAK; select_conn() picks max score where score = c->window / (c->in_flight_pkts + 1); CONN_TIMEOUT 4s, GLOBAL_TIMEOUT 10s, IDLE_TIME 1s keepalive, PKT_LOG_SZ 256, SEND_BUF_SIZE 8MB.

options.name: srtla_rec (C) — the reference receiver
options.natTraversal: Accepts any source address that presents a known group ID — which is exactly how it survives per-path NAT and carrier rebinding
options.androidSupport: n/a
options.verdict: reject. Upstream says outright it is 'unsupported, no longer under development and not suitable for production deployment.' Also: MAX_CONNS_PER_GROUP 8, MAX_GROUPS 200, CONN_TIMEOUT/GROUP_TIMEOUT 10s, CLEANUP_PERIOD 3s, and NO authentication whatsoever — possession of the 256-byte group ID is the only credential.

options.name: irlserver/irl-srt-server (SLS fork)
options.natTraversal: Single public UDP listener; SRTLA publishers on a dedicated listen_publisher_srtla port
options.androidSupport: n/a (server)
options.verdict: adopt as the relay base. MIT, ~442 commits, active CI, SRTLA receive + SRT live server + streamid-based publisher/player identity + extended HTTP stats/control API. Caveat: it requires the IRL-maintained SRT fork on the 'belabox' branch, not upstream Haivision, and it is MPEG-TS in/out — you add the RTMP fan-out yourself.

options.name: irlserver/srtla_send (Rust)
options.androidSupport: no bindings
options.desktopSupport: Unix/Linux/Windows, requires Rust nightly + source routing
options.verdict: prototype / mine for ideas. MIT license makes its scheduler legally reusable, unlike the AGPL original: exponential NAK decay (~8s recovery), NAK-burst detection (>=5 NAKs in 3s -> 0.7x score multiplier), RTT-aware selection (3% max bonus for lower RTT), stalled-link deselect. Self-labelled experimental; no FFI or mobile story.

options.name: Brix (Android, Kotlin)
options.androidSupport: yes — this is the existence proof
options.verdict: do not link, do read. The load-bearing fact: 'The SRT and SRTLA client is written from scratch in Kotlin; it is not a wrapper around libsrt.' So a pure-JVM SRTLA sender on Android is demonstrably possible. But ~29 commits, self-described beta, tested on one device (Samsung S21/Android 15), thermal critical at 1080p in six minutes, 1.5–2.5h battery. GPL-3.0 rules it out as a dependency for a proprietary APK.

options.name: Moblin (iOS)
options.license: open source (repo public; confirm exact SPDX before reuse)
options.iosSupport: yes — ships SRT, SRTLA, RIST, WHIP, RTMP/S from an iPhone
options.androidSupport: no
options.verdict: study, do not fork. Its README states the single most important constraint in this whole report: 'Can use one cellular, one WiFi and multiple Ethernet connections simultaneously.' One cellular. Also useful: adaptive bitrate for SRT(LA)/RIST/RTMP, per-connection upload stats, connection priorities, and it cannot capture video in background (freezes a frame).

options.name: Moblink / moblink-rust — spare phone as an extra path
options.natTraversal: WebSocket control plane (manual URL or mDNS discovery) + UDP data relay over the relay device's own interface; mDNS is unreliable across NAT
options.androidSupport: yes (Rust reimplementation matches the Android auth handshake)
options.verdict: adopt the pattern. This is the industry's actual answer to the one-cellular-per-phone constraint: a second handset joins over local Wi-Fi, authenticates by challenge-response, opens a local UDP socket on its own cellular, and forwards bidirectionally. MIT-licensed, so directly reusable.

options.name: RIST Main Profile (VSF TR-06-2) / libRIST
options.license: libRIST: BSD-2-Clause (VideoLAN/SipRadius). Spec: freely published by VSF.
options.natTraversal: GRE-over-UDP on a single port — same outbound-only story as SRTLA
options.androidSupport: C library, buildable via NDK
options.verdict: the serious alternative to SRTLA, and the only one that is a real open standard. Main Profile has bonding, dynamic load sharing, mixing of different link types, retransmission throttling, PSK AES-CTR encryption and EAP-SRP authentication — i.e. it fixes SRTLA's missing auth at the protocol layer. BSD-2-Clause beats AGPL-3.0 outright. Cost: far smaller IRL ecosystem, and you lose interop with the Moblin/IRL Pro/BELABOX installed base.

options.name: Speedify SDK (channel bonding VPN)
options.license: proprietary, OEM license, price on application (partners cited: Comcast, Cox, Xfinity, CUJO AI, OmniAccess)
options.iosSupport: yes, but as a VPN — on iOS that means a Network Extension entitlement
options.androidSupport: yes, VpnService-shaped
options.verdict: reject for LIVETAP. Architecturally it is a bonding VPN: client splits packets across up to 8 parallel sockets per link, AES-256/ChaCha20 over DTLS, server reassembles in order and forwards. Two disqualifiers: it is transport-agnostic so it cannot use video semantics (no I-frame priority, no encoder feedback), and Redundant Mode — the mode you actually want for live — 'caps your speed at your fastest single connection', i.e. it stops being bonding. Plus you would be reselling someone else's relay under someone else's licence.

options.name: LiveU LRT + LU-Smart
options.license: proprietary, patented (LiveU claims to be the inventor and patent holder of cellular bonding)
options.natTraversal: client→LiveU decoding servers (physical or cloud), managed via LiveU Central
options.iosSupport: yes — LU-Smart runs on iOS and Android
options.androidSupport: yes
options.verdict: reject as a dependency, respect as a competitor and as prior art. LU-Smart bonds the handset's internal Wi-Fi + 4G/5G, and to get a SECOND cellular path it requires an external MiFi — independent confirmation of the one-modem-per-phone constraint. LRT = dynamic FEC (more redundancy as errors rise), group ACK + selective retransmit, packet prioritisation, adaptive bitrate. The patent estate is a real commercial risk surface for anything you describe as 'cellular bonding'.

options.name: Teradek Bond II + Sputnik server
options.license: proprietary; Sputnik distributed as a self-hostable Linux server / EC2 AMI / 'Preconfigured Sputnik Server' appliance
options.natTraversal: 'a single, publicly addressable port' — same one-public-endpoint model as everyone else
options.androidSupport: n/a
options.verdict: reject as tech, copy the deployment model. Up to six cellular modems into one H.264 encode, recombined by Sputnik, plus ABRS adaptive bitrate. The interesting product lesson is that Teradek sells the relay three ways — bring-your-own EC2, buy our appliance, or buy Base — because customers refuse to depend on a vendor cloud for live.

options.name: Peplink SpeedFusion
options.androidSupport: no
options.verdict: reject, but steal the vocabulary. It separates three distinct behaviours that LIVETAP should also separate and name: Bandwidth Bonding (packet-level aggregation, any single session gets the combined capacity), WAN Smoothing (duplicate critical packets so tunnel latency becomes that of the FASTEST link), and FEC with published overhead tiers — adaptive 6–20%, low ~13%, high ~26%. Those overhead numbers are the most useful public data point for sizing your own redundancy budget.

options.name: MPTCP (RFC 8684)
options.natTraversal: TCP option 30 is routinely stripped or rewritten to NOOP by middleboxes; falls back to plain TCP silently
options.androidSupport: partial, historically via carrier SOCKS proxies (Samsung S6 era)
options.verdict: reject. It is TCP: head-of-line blocking and a reliability model you cannot override, which is the exact thing live video must be able to opt out of. Silent middlebox fallback also means you cannot tell the user whether they are bonded.

options.name: Multipath QUIC (draft-ietf-quic-multipath)
options.natTraversal: good in principle (UDP, connection IDs survive path change)
options.androidSupport: no shipping stack
options.verdict: reject for now, revisit in 2027. As of the 2026-01-12 datatracker state it is still an Active Internet-Draft at rev -21, IESG 'Waiting for AD Go-Ahead::AD Followup' — not an RFC. Per-path congestion control is specified, but there is no mobile-shippable implementation and no relay ecosystem. This is the option that sounds advanced and would cost you a year.

options.name: SRT itself (Haivision libsrt)
options.license: MPL-2.0 — permissive, static linking allowed, explicitly relicensed from LGPL-2.1 to enable mobile integration, no royalties
options.androidSupport: yes — and RootEncoder (your existing Android stack) already speaks SRT natively in Java/Kotlin
options.verdict: adopt. This is the one piece you can take wholesale with no licensing pain. Note the receiver-side gotcha: BELABOX and irl-srt-server both require a PATCHED SRT fork, because out-of-order arrival across bonded paths triggers retransmission storms in stock libsrt.

hardConstraints: ONE PHONE = ONE CELLULAR PATH. This is the constraint that reshapes the product. iOS does not support Dual SIM Dual Active at all — DSDS keeps both SIMs registered but only one carries data at a time. Moblin's README states the achievable set exactly: 'Can use one cellular, one WiFi and multiple Ethernet connections simultaneously.' LiveU's own LU-Smart page confirms it from the commercial side: to bond two cellular connections in a single smartphone you must add an external MiFi. So the honest mobile pitch is 'Wi-Fi + cellular', not 'Wi-Fi + 5G + LTE'. Sources: https://github.com/eerimoq/moblin/blob/main/README.md , https://www.liveu.tv/products/create/lu-smart , https://discussions.apple.com/thread/254870893

NO BONDING FROM THE WEBVIEW. Nothing in a Capacitor/WebView JS context can bind a socket to a named network interface. On Android this requires ConnectivityManager.requestNetwork(NetworkRequest with addTransportType(TRANSPORT_CELLULAR) + addCapability(NET_CAPABILITY_INTERNET)) plus the CHANGE_NETWORK_STATE permission, then Network.bindSocket(DatagramSocket) or the Network's SocketFactory, per socket. Crucially, requestNetwork brings a network UP but does not move existing sockets onto it. LIVETAP Bond is a native Capacitor plugin or it does not exist. Sources: https://developer.android.com/develop/connectivity/network-ops/reading-network-state , https://developer.android.com/training/monitoring-device-state/connectivity-status-type

iOS DEFAULTS TO WI-FI AND WILL FIGHT YOU. You must set NWParameters.requiredInterfaceType = .cellular (Network.framework, iOS 12+) or IP_BOUND_IF / IPV6_BOUND_IF on a BSD socket. Multiple developer reports describe iOS still routing via Wi-Fi when Wi-Fi is on despite requiredInterfaceType being set. Budget real engineering time for a 'is this path actually on cellular' verification step, and do not claim a path is bonded until you have proven its egress IP differs. Sources: https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/795093 , https://github.com/twilio/voice-quickstart-ios/issues/318

SRTLA IS AGPL-3.0, AND §13 CATCHES THE RELAY. github.com/BELABOX/srtla is AGPL-3.0. That is fatal twice over for a commercial LIVETAP: linking it into a proprietary app binary is a GPL-family violation, and running srtla_rec as a network service triggers AGPL's remote-network-interaction clause, obliging you to offer the complete corresponding source of your relay to its users. The MIT-licensed alternatives (irlserver/irl-srt-server, irlserver/srtla_send) and the BSD-2-Clause libRIST exist precisely because of this. Source: https://api.github.com/repos/BELABOX/srtla

THE REFERENCE RECEIVER IS ABANDONED ON PURPOSE. BELABOX's own README: srtla_rec is 'unsupported, no longer under development and not suitable for production deployment.' Every production SRTLA relay in the wild is a third-party reimplementation. Do not build on srtla_rec. Source: https://github.com/BELABOX/srtla/blob/main/README.md

SRTLA HAS NO AUTHENTICATION. In srtla_rec, the only credential is the 256-byte group ID: a sender presenting a known ID from any source address is admitted to that group. There is no key, no signature, no access control. Hard caps are MAX_CONNS_PER_GROUP = 8 and MAX_GROUPS = 200 per receiver, with 10s connection and group timeouts. If LIVETAP adopts SRTLA verbatim, you MUST add your own auth layer (SRT streamid + a server-side token check, as irl-srt-server does) before it touches the public internet. Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BELABOX/srtla/main/srtla_rec.c

THE RELAY CANNOT RUN ON VERCEL, OR ON ANY SERVERLESS PLATFORM. A bonding relay needs a long-lived process holding a single publicly addressable UDP port on a static IP, with per-group in-memory reassembly state across multiple source addresses. No UDP, no static ingress port, no long-lived sockets, no sticky state on serverless. Teradek states the same requirement for Sputnik ('a single, publicly addressable port', static public IP). This is a VPS/bare-metal workload. Source: https://teradek.com/products/sputnik-server

NAT TRAVERSAL IS NOT YOUR PROBLEM — PER-PATH IDENTITY IS. Every bonded path is a client-initiated outbound UDP flow to one public relay; no STUN, no TURN, no ICE, no hole punching, works behind CGNAT. But each path egresses from a DIFFERENT public IP (different carrier, different NAT), and a carrier can rebind a path's port mid-stream. So path→session binding must be in-band. SRTLA's answer is the three-way registration: sender REG1 (random half-ID) → receiver REG2 (mixed ID) → sender REG2 → receiver REG3, with error codes REG_ERR / REG_NAK / REG_NGP. The receiver also tracks last_addr so a returning peer on a changed address rejoins its group. Source: https://github.com/BELABOX/srtla/blob/main/README.md , https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BELABOX/srtla/main/common.h

BONDING COSTS 1–2.5 SECONDS OF BUFFER, AND THAT IS NOT NEGOTIABLE. Single-path SRT wants latency >= 4x RTT. Bonded SRTLA needs 1500–3000 ms, with the standard advice being 'start at 2000 ms and reduce only after observing actual RTT and jitter', and 2500–3500 ms in congested venues. The reason is structural: the receiver cannot release a packet until the SLOWEST contributing path has had its chance, so aggregate jitter is strictly worse than any single path. LiveU, with a decade of proprietary work, gets LRT to ~0.8 s and 450 ms glass-to-glass point-to-point — treat that as the floor, not your target. Sources: https://vajracast.com/blog/srtla-bonding-belabox-guide/ , https://www.liveu.tv/solutions/lrt , https://get.liveu.tv/point-to-point/

YOU CANNOT ENCODE AT THE AGGREGATE BITRATE. Field guidance is to keep encoding bitrate below ~70% of measured aggregate capacity, because retransmission and FEC need the headroom. Peplink publishes its FEC overhead tiers openly: adaptive 6–20%, low ~13%, high ~26%. So '3 links x 5 Mbps = 15 Mbps of video' is a lie you must not put in the UI. Sources: https://vajracast.com/blog/srtla-bonding-belabox-guide/ , https://connectivity101.com/docs/speedfusion/profiles/

STOCK libsrt MISBEHAVES AS A BONDING RECEIVER. Both BELABOX and irl-srt-server require a patched SRT fork (irl-srt-server names the 'belabox' branch specifically) because normal out-of-order arrival across paths provokes excessive retransmission requests. Budget for maintaining a forked libsrt on the relay, indefinitely. Sources: https://github.com/BELABOX/srtla/blob/main/README.md , https://github.com/irlserver/irl-srt-server

MULTIPATH QUIC IS NOT A STANDARD YET. draft-ietf-quic-multipath was still an Active Internet-Draft at rev -21 as of 2026-01-12, IESG state 'Waiting for AD Go-Ahead::AD Followup'. No RFC number, no shipping mobile stack, no relay ecosystem. Source: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-quic-multipath

MPTCP IS THE WRONG LAYER AND FAILS SILENTLY. RFC 8684 is TCP — head-of-line blocking and mandatory reliability, both wrong for live video — and middleboxes routinely strip TCP option 30, at which point iOS silently falls back to single-path TCP with no signal to the app. Sources: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8684 , https://support.apple.com/en-us/101905

THERMAL AND BATTERY ARE THE REAL MOBILE CEILING, NOT NETWORKING. Brix reports critical thermal throttling at 1080p within six minutes and 1.5–2.5 hour sessions on a Samsung S21. Running a second radio full-tilt alongside the encoder makes this worse, not better. Moblin also notes iOS cannot capture video in the background — it freezes a frame. Sources: https://github.com/0rb1ta/Brix , https://github.com/eerimoq/moblin/blob/main/README.md

THE PRICE OF THIS FEATURE IS ALREADY SET AT ~$10/MONTH. BELABOX Cloud's SRTLA relay is $10/month; IRLServer is $9.99/month with unlimited bandwidth. That price is only achievable on unmetered bare metal — at AWS's ~$0.09/GB egress, a single 6 Mbps stream fanned out to three destinations burns roughly 8 GB/hour of egress, i.e. about $0.70/hour, which destroys the unit economics before you have paid for anything else. Host the relay on flat-rate-bandwidth providers. Sources: https://irlserver.com/pricing , https://github.com/BELABOX/srtla
report.recommendation:
Build LIVETAP Bond as a clean-room SRTLA-v2-compatible sender in your NATIVE layers, and run an MIT-licensed relay you own. Concretely, in order:

1. RELAY FIRST, ON A VPS, NOT VERCEL. Fork irlserver/irl-srt-server (MIT) plus its belabox-branch libsrt. It already terminates SRTLA on a dedicated publisher port, identifies streams by SRT streamid, and exposes an HTTP stats/control API. Add two things it lacks: real token auth keyed on streamid (SRTLA has none — see hard constraints), and the RTMP fan-out to YouTube/Twitch, which you already do in the desktop app. Host on flat-bandwidth bare metal; the $10/month market price does not survive hyperscaler egress. One public UDP port, static IP, per-group reassembly state in RAM.

2. DESKTOP (ELECTRON) AS THE PROVING GROUND, BECAUSE IT IS CHEAPEST. Node's dgram lets you socket.bind({address: <source IP>}) per interface, which is exactly the primitive srtla_send relies on. You can stand up a real 2-path bond over Ethernet + Wi-Fi with no native code and verify it against your relay using the harness you already have in infra/dev-harness/broadcast. Do this before touching mobile.

3. IMPLEMENT THE SCHEDULER FROM THE MIT RUST PORT, NOT THE AGPL C. Start with score = window / (in_flight + 1), WINDOW_DEF 20 / MIN 1 / MAX 60, +30 on ACK, -100 on NAK, 1s keepalive, 4s per-link and 10s global timeouts. Then layer irlserver/srtla_send's MIT improvements: exponential NAK decay (~8s), NAK-burst penalty (>=5 NAKs in 3s → 0.7x), small RTT bonus (<=3%), and stalled-link deselect. Set the SRT latency buffer to 2000 ms by default, expose 1500–3000 ms, and cap the encoder at 70% of measured aggregate.

4. MOBILE LAST, AND SCOPE IT HONESTLY AS WI-FI + CELLULAR. Android: a Capacitor plugin doing requestNetwork(TRANSPORT_CELLULAR) + Network.bindSocket per path, with CHANGE_NETWORK_STATE and a foreground service; RootEncoder already gives you SRT, so you are adding the SRTLA shim, not a stack. Brix proves this is doable in pure Kotlin. iOS: NWParameters.requiredInterfaceType and verify empirically that the path really egresses on cellular. Then ship the Moblink pattern (MIT, directly reusable) as the answer to "I want three paths": a second handset joins over local Wi-Fi via WebSocket + challenge-response and relays UDP over its own modem. That is what the entire industry does, including LiveU, which sells you a MiFi for the same reason.

5. ON THE UI, SAY THE THING NOBODY SAYS. Everyone shows per-connection upload bitrate, RTT, connection count, and a dropped-packet counter (belaUI, Moblin, Vajracast's dashboard). Everyone HIDES the scheduler's actual state — per-link window, in-flight packets, which link carried which packet, NAK bursts — and, more importantly, hides the latency budget the user just bought and the fact that usable bitrate is ~70% of the sum, not the sum. LIVETAP's differentiator is the same one you already shipped in "the desktop app stops claiming to broadcast when it cannot": show the added delay in seconds, show aggregate USABLE capacity rather than raw sum, and mark a path as bonded only after you have verified a distinct egress IP.

Only choose RIST Main Profile over SRTLA if standards-compliance and built-in EAP-SRP auth + PSK encryption matter more to you than interoperating with the Moblin / IRL Pro / BELABOX installed base. libRIST is BSD-2-Clause, which is the cleanest licence in this entire report. Reject Speedify (OEM licence, VPN-shaped, and its Redundant Mode caps you at your fastest single link, which is not bonding), reject MPTCP, and revisit Multipath QUIC no earlier than 2027.
uncertainties: Clean-room risk: I am recommending you reimplement an AGPL-3.0 protocol. The wire format and constants are published in public headers and the SRTLA v2 handshake is described in the README, and Brix independently reimplemented the client in Kotlin — but 'read the AGPL source, then write your own' is legally grey. Get counsel, or negotiate a commercial licence with BELABOX (single-vendor copyright makes dual-licensing plausible), or take RIST/libRIST under BSD-2-Clause and sidestep the question entirely.
Moblin's exact SPDX licence was not confirmed from the README — I only verified the repo is public. Confirm before reusing any of it. Moblink-rust's MIT is confirmed.

Whether binding a UDP socket to a source IP on Windows reliably selects that interface for EGRESS is not verified. On Linux, srtla explicitly requires OS-level source routing on top of bind(), which implies bind() alone is insufficient there. Test this early on the Electron path — it could invalidate step 2 of the recommendation.

Teradek Sputnik is described in third-party material as using 'a single publicly addressable TCP port'. I could not confirm from Teradek whether media is TCP or whether that refers only to a control channel. Do not cite it as evidence about transport choice.

The AWS egress cost figure (~8 GB/hour for one 6 Mbps stream fanned to three destinations, ~$0.70/hour) is my arithmetic from published $/GB rates plus an assumed ~25% SRTLA/retransmission overhead, not a measured number. The $9.99 and $10 relay prices are sourced.

Android's requestNetwork(TRANSPORT_CELLULAR) behaviour while Wi-Fi is the default network is confirmed as the correct API but I found no authoritative statement on device-by-device reliability, carrier 'mobile data always active' dependencies, or whether Android 14/15/16 foreground-service-type rules add friction. Verify on real hardware across at least three OEMs before promising it.

LiveU holds patents and publicly claims to be the inventor and patent holder of cellular bonding. I did not enumerate the patents or assess whether any read on an SRTLA-style implementation. If LIVETAP Bond becomes a marketed feature, this needs a freedom-to-operate review, not a research report.

I did not verify whether irl-srt-server's HTTP control API is sufficient for per-user auth at your scale, nor its behaviour under concurrent groups approaching the 200-group / 8-connection-per-group ceilings that SRTLA's reference receiver imposes.

verdict.claim: That LIVETAP Bond should be built by (1) forking irlserver/irl-srt-server (MIT) + its belabox-branch libsrt to get an MIT-licensed relay that "already terminates SRTLA," adding only token auth and RTMP fan-out; (2) proving the bond on Electron with no native code because Node's `dgram` `socket.bind({address})` is "exactly the primitive srtla_send relies on"; (3) copying the scheduler from the "MIT Rust port" irlserver/srtla_send rather than the AGPL C, as a "clean-room" sender; with Multipath QUIC deferred to 2027 as a non-standard draft.
verdict.reasoning:
Four load-bearing claims fail against primary sources. I cloned and read the repos rather than trusting the READMEs' framing.

1. THE RELAY DOES NOT TERMINATE SRTLA. irl-srt-server contains zero SRTLA protocol code. Grepping all of src/ for "srtla" returns only a config directive (`listen_publisher_srtla`), a boolean `m_is_srtla_listener`, and one sockopt: `srt_setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SRTO_SRTLAPATCHES, ...)` in src/core/SLSSrt.cpp:287. No REG1/REG2/REG3, no group table, no per-link reassembly. Their own README line 154 spells out the topology: `listen_publisher_srtla 4002;      # SRTLA/bonded (via srtla_rec)`, and line 175 says the "patches" merely "disable dynamic reorder tolerance and periodic NAK reports." The libsrt fork is a reorder-tolerance patch (`SRT_HAVE_SRTLA_REORDER_HOLD`, `msSrtlaReorderHold` in SLSManager.cpp:465-472), not a bonding stack. The bonding is done upstream by BELABOX's `srtla_rec` — the exact binary the report itself says is AGPL and "abandoned on purpose." The researcher recommended the MIT wrapper and assumed it was the bonding layer.

2. THERE IS NO MAINTAINED PERMISSIVE SRTLA RECEIVER — INCLUDING AT IRLSERVER. `gh api orgs/irlserver/repos` shows IRLServer maintains **irlserver/srtla, license=AGPL-3.0, parent=BELABOX/srtla, pushed 2026-09-09** — six days ago. The vendor held up as the MIT path runs AGPL srtla_rec in production. Every other receiver is AGPL too: e04/go-irl (AGPL-3.0, 80 stars, pushed 2026-09-08 — a from-scratch Go rewrite that still chose AGPL), manueldev/srtla-windows and Bohdan177/srtla-windows (both AGPL-3.0). The sole permissive one, yannismate/srtla-rs (MIT), has 5 stars, no README, and is stale since 2025-01-15. Adopting the recommended architecture therefore puts an AGPL-3.0 network service on LIVETAP's relay — triggering the §13 obligation the report itself called "fatal."

3. THE "MIT RUST PORT" IS A LINE-CITED TRANSLATION OF THE AGPL C, NOT CLEAN-ROOM. srtla_send/LICENSE is "MIT / Copyright (c) 2025 Thomas Lekanger," but the source documents its own derivation: crates/srtla-core/src/connection/congestion/classic.rs:1 "Classic congestion control matching original C implementation"; :13 "Matches C implementation lines 291-293"; :16 "CLASSIC MODE: Exact C implementation"; :24 "Note: WINDOW_INCR - 1 in C code". Also selection/classic.rs:19 "matches the original C implementation's behavior exactly", srtla-protocol/src/parsers.rs:261 "The C code does: uint32_t *acks = (uint32_t *)buf; for (int i = 1; ...)". Every constant matches BELABOX/srtla/srtla_send.c:47-52 (WINDOW_MIN 1, WINDOW_DEF 20, WINDOW_MAX 60, WINDOW_MULT 1000, WINDOW_DECR 100, WINDOW_INCR 30). Citing an AGPL file by line number while transcribing it is the documentary opposite of clean-room; a downstream MIT grant cannot extinguish BELABOX's copyright in the derived expression. Step 3 of the recommendation ("implement the scheduler from the MIT Rust port") directly contradicts step 0 ("build a clean-room sender").

4. THE NODE `dgram` PROVING GROUND IS PLATFORM-LUCK, AND YOUR DEV BOX IS THE LUCKY PLATFORM. BELABOX's own README states the prerequisite the report omitted: "The sender needs to have **source routing** configured, as srtla uses `bind()` to map UDP sockets to a given connection. **Only Linux is supported**." `bind()` to a source IP is necessary but not sufficient — under Linux's default weak host model the kernel routes by destination, so a socket bound to the Wi-Fi address will egress the Ethernet default route carrying a foreign source IP, which upstream BCP38/uRPF drops. Windows Vista+ defaults to **strong host send**, which does constrain egress to the address-owning interface. LIVETAP develops on Windows Server 2022, so the two-path bond will appear to verify in infra/dev-harness/broadcast and then silently collapse to one path on Linux and macOS. Node cannot fix it: nodejs.org/api/dgram.html exposes only setBroadcast/setTTL/setMulticastTTL/setMulticastLoopback/setMulticastInterface/setRecvBufferSize/setSendBufferSize — no SO_BINDTODEVICE, no IP_BOUND_IF, and no generic setsockopt escape hatch. Policy routing also needs admin/root, which an Electron app cannot assume. "No native code" is false on 2 of 3 desktop platforms.

5. SMALLER ERRORS THAT SHOW THE REPO WAS NOT READ. The report says to "add two things it lacks: real token auth keyed on streamid... and the RTMP fan-out." irl-srt-server's CONFIGURATION.md already ships publish-auth webhooks, "Player key authentication" (player_key_auth_url, rate limits, caching), streamid routing, IP allow/deny, and "Push destinations" driven by the publish auth webhook. What it actually lacks is RTMP specifically — `push_destination_allow_schemes` defaults to `srt` only. Separately, streamid auth cannot fix "SRTLA has no authentication": the SRT handshake happens *after* srtla_rec has already admitted the unauthenticated bonding group and allocated reassembly state, so the auth must go in the receiver they don't control.

6. MULTIPATH QUIC IS STALE BY EIGHT MONTHS. draft-ietf-quic-multipath is at rev -21 dated 2026-03-17 and is now in the **RFC Editor Queue** ("Submitted to IESG for Publication," "Awaiting First editor") — it has cleared IESG, not "Waiting for AD Go-Ahead::AD Followup" as of 2026-01-12. It is an approved Standards-Track document awaiting an RFC number. The practical conclusion (no shipping mobile stack, no relay ecosystem) still holds, but "revisit no earlier than 2027" rests on a stale fact.

WHAT SURVIVED: Moblin (MIT) and Moblink (MIT) are confirmed permissive and actively maintained (pushed 2026-09-14 / 2026-09-05), so the second-handset pattern is reusable. CHANGE_NETWORK_STATE was restored to protection level "normal" (android.googlesource.com/platform/frameworks/base d542705), so the Android plugin permission story holds. MAX_CONNS_PER_GROUP 8 / MAX_GROUPS 200 verified at srtla_rec.c:34-35. irlserver/srt is MPL-2.0, which is genuinely linkable.
verdict.correction:
The relay is not MIT where it counts, and the sender is not clean-room. Actual position:

- Forking irl-srt-server gives you an SRT ingest/auth/push server with a reorder-tolerance patch. It gives you **no bonding**. You must still supply an SRTLA receiver, and every maintained one on earth is AGPL-3.0 (BELABOX/srtla; irlserver/srtla; e04/go-irl). So the choice is honest, not clever: (a) write a genuine clean-room SRTLA receiver from the wire protocol described in BELABOX's README — REG1/REG2/REG3, SRTLA_REG_ERR/NAK/NGP, last_addr rebinding — with nobody on the team having read srtla_rec.c or the Rust transcription of it; (b) accept AGPL-3.0 on the relay process and publish the relay's corresponding source (§13 reaches the relay, not your desktop/mobile apps, so this is survivable if the relay is a thin service); or (c) use RIST Main Profile via libRIST (BSD-2-Clause) and skip the licence problem entirely.

- Option (c) is stronger than the report allows. IRLServer — the same vendor cited as the SRTLA authority — now maintains **irlserver/librist (BSD-2-Clause, pushed 2026-07-17)** and **irlserver/librist-rust (MIT, pushed 2026-05-20)**. The incumbent is hedging toward RIST. RIST Main Profile also brings the EAP-SRP auth and PSK encryption that SRTLA structurally lacks, removing the need to bolt auth onto a protocol that has none. The only real cost is losing drop-in compatibility with the Moblin/IRL Pro/BELABOX installed base — which matters only if importing those users is a launch requirement.

- Do not copy constants or structure from irlserver/srtla_send. Cite-by-line-number comments in that repo make derivation provable. Either work from the protocol description only, or treat the AGPL as binding.

- The desktop proving ground needs native code on day one, not day thirty. Budget SO_BINDTODEVICE (Linux, needs CAP_NET_RAW or root) or per-interface policy routing via `ip rule`/`ip route`, and IP_BOUND_IF on macOS, as a native Electron addon. Your Windows-only green test is a false positive caused by the strong host send model. Add a pre-flight that resolves each path's public egress IP via a distinct-source check before labelling anything bonded — and expect it to report "not bonded" on Linux with no explanation until the routing is fixed, because BCP38 filtering drops the spoofed-source packets before any reply comes back.

- irl-srt-server already has streamid/publish-auth webhooks and push destinations; the only real gap is that push schemes default to `srt` and you need RTMP. Scope that as a small patch, not a workstream. And note the README: "not supported on Windows."

- Multipath QUIC is in the RFC Editor Queue as of rev -21 (2026-03-17). Still not deployable, but re-check in 2026, not 2027.

report.summary: The single most dangerous fact for LIVETAP: srtla — the only production-proven RTMP/SRT bonding implementation, the thing BELABOX/IRL streaming runs on — is AGPL-3.0. Linking srtla_send into the app is distribution of AGPL code and would relicense LIVETAP; running a modified srtla_rec on the LIVETAP relay triggers AGPL §13's network-source obligation. Meanwhile SRT's own MPL-2.0 bonding cannot replace it: `broadcast` mode costs "another 100% overhead" per link and `balancing` mode is marked UNDER DEVELOPMENT in Haivision's own docs. Multipath QUIC is still not an RFC (draft-ietf-quic-multipath-21, submitted to IESG, awaiting AD go-ahead), but its MIT/BSD implementations (picoquic, quiche) are the only permissively-licensed path to real capacity aggregation. Two constraints will shape the product regardless of transport: iOS forbids aggregate multipath in App Store builds, and a bonded 6 Mbps stream burns ~2.7 GB/hour — roughly 1.4x Speedify's entire default monthly cellular budget, per hour.

options.maturity: production — the de-facto IRL bonding standard
options.license: AGPL-3.0 (confirmed: LICENSE header reads 'GNU AFFERO GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE Version 3'; GitHub SPDX = agpl-3.0)
options.natTraversal: client-initiated UDP to a known relay; no ICE/STUN. Works behind NAT, no inbound needed.
options.androidSupport: C, cross-compiles; BELABOX runs it on Linux SBCs. No Android port shipped by upstream.
options.verdict: REJECT outright for an MIT product — AGPL-3.0 infects the client app on distribution and the relay under §13; it is also cryptographically unauthenticated (see hard constraints).

options.name: SRT (Haivision) — core protocol
options.androidSupport: yes — builds via NDK; RootEncoder (already in LIVETAP's stack, Apache-2.0) exposes SRT
options.desktopSupport: yes (Win/macOS/Linux) — this is what the Electron app can use
options.verdict: ADOPT for relay→CDN and as the single-path fallback. MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft: Mozilla's FAQ Q11/Q13 confirm you may link it into an MIT/proprietary larger work; you only must publish changes to MPL files themselves.

options.name: SRT connection bonding (socket groups)
options.maturity: broadcast + backup production; BALANCING mode explicitly 'UNDER DEVELOPMENT'; multicast 'CONCEPT! NOT IMPLEMENTED!'
options.androidSupport: builds, but balancing mode is not production-safe
options.verdict: REJECT as the aggregation engine. Broadcast mode duplicates the full payload on every link — 'every next link in this group gives then another 100% overhead' — which doubles cellular cost. Balancing (the only true aggregation mode) is not finished. This gap is precisely why srtla exists.

options.name: picoquic
options.maturity: research-grade but actively maintained; the reference implementation the multipath draft was prototyped against
options.natTraversal: QUIC path validation via PATH_CHALLENGE/PATH_RESPONSE (RFC 9000 §8.2); client→relay, no inbound
options.androidSupport: C, NDK-buildable; no first-party Android bindings — you own the JNI layer
options.iosSupport: C, buildable; you own the bridge
options.verdict: PROTOTYPE — MIT-clean and the closest thing to a reference multipath QUIC. Budget real effort for the mobile build and bindings; nobody has done that work for you.

options.name: quiche (Cloudflare)
options.maturity: production for HTTP/3; has internal PathMap/path management, multipath extension is not a stable supported feature
options.natTraversal: QUIC path validation; C FFI available
options.androidSupport: Rust + C FFI; Android builds are done in the wild (e.g. Kotlin Multiplatform bindings exist) but not first-party supported
options.verdict: PROTOTYPE — license is ideal (BSD-2), maintenance is excellent, but do not assume draft-21 multipath is there and supported. Verify against the current tree before committing.

options.name: msquic (Microsoft)
options.androidSupport: yes, officially supported platform
options.verdict: REJECT for Bond v1 — maintainers state msquic does not support multipath QUIC and there is no official timeline; only an unreviewed external draft PR. Great QUIC, wrong feature.

options.name: quinn (Rust)
options.license: MIT OR Apache-2.0 (Cargo.toml: license = "MIT OR Apache-2.0"; GitHub surfaces only apache-2.0)
options.androidSupport: Rust cross-compiles; no first-party mobile story
options.verdict: REJECT for v1 — no multipath. Note the GitHub license badge is misleading; the crate is genuinely dual MIT/Apache, so take it under MIT.

options.name: lsquic (LiteSpeed)
options.androidSupport: listed as a supported platform
options.verdict: REJECT for v1 — no multipath extension. Worth keeping as a QUIC fallback given its Android support.

options.name: mvfst (Meta)
options.androidSupport: used inside Meta mobile apps but the OSS build is heavy (folly dependency)
options.verdict: REJECT — license fine, but the folly/Buck dependency chain is a maintenance tax a small team should not take on.

options.name: libdatachannel
options.maturity: production, actively maintained; WebRTC DataChannel + media + WebSocket
options.license: MPL-2.0 since v0.18 (was LGPLv2.1+ before — check which version you vendor)

options.androidSupport: officially supported platform

options.license: GPL-2.0 — both the Linux kernel module and wireguard-nt
options.natTraversal: roaming endpoints, but no built-in multipath
options.androidSupport: kernel/VPNService — requires the VPN API, system-wide

options.name: wireguard-go / BoringTun
options.maturity: production (wireguard-go is the reference userspace impl; BoringTun is Cloudflare's Rust one)
options.androidSupport: wireguard-go powers the official Android app via VPNService
options.verdict: REJECT as a transport, but MINE IT FOR DESIGN. WireGuard's crypto construction — Noise_IKpsk2, ChaCha20-Poly1305, 1-RTT, static-key-pinned peer — is exactly the right shape for authenticating a client to a known relay, and both licenses are MIT-compatible.

options.name: Noise Protocol (IK) via libsodium
options.maturity: production — this is what WireGuard ships
options.license: libsodium: ISC (note: GitHub's API returns NOASSERTION/'Other', but the LICENSE file is ISC). Noise is a spec, not code.
options.natTraversal: n/a — you build it on your own UDP framing
options.androidSupport: libsodium has first-class Android NDK builds

options.name: DTLS 1.3 (RFC 9147)
options.maturity: spec is final; library support is the problem
options.license: depends on library — OpenSSL 3.0+/BoringSSL are Apache-2.0; wolfSSL is GPLv2-or-commercial (verify before use)
