DTLS 1.3 lands in OpenSSL 4.1 in October 2026 — today only 4.1.0-alpha1 (2026-09-09) exists, and DTLSv1_listen() does not support DTLS 1.3 (you must use SSL_new_listener()). The mature alternative is wolfSSL, whose GPLv2/commercial dual license is an MIT landmine.

options.name: DTLS 1.2 + Connection ID (RFC 9146)
options.androidSupport: yes
options.verdict: REJECT — the RFC disqualifies itself for this use case: 'The lack of a CID update mechanism in DTLS 1.2 makes this extension unsuitable for mobility scenarios where correlation must be considered,' and it says users SHOULD refuse CIDs in DTLS 1.2 and switch to DTLS 1.3.

options.name: QUIC + TLS 1.3 (RFC 9001) + multipath extension
options.maturity: QUIC v1 is RFC 9000 and production everywhere; multipath is draft-21, IESG queue, NOT yet an RFC
options.natTraversal: PATH_CHALLENGE/PATH_RESPONSE path validation, 3x anti-amplification limit, per-path connection IDs
options.androidSupport: pair with ConnectivityManager.requestNetwork + Network.bindSocket per path
options.iosSupport: pair with NWParameters.requiredInterfaceType = .cellular per path (in-app multipath is allowed; OS aggregate multipath is not)
options.verdict: ADOPT the design, PROTOTYPE the code. You get authenticated encryption, key update, path validation, amplification limits, and per-path packet number spaces for free — every one of which you would otherwise get wrong by hand.

options.name: irl-srt-server (SLS fork with SRTLA)
options.license: GitHub SPDX reports MIT — but the README says it 'adds SRTLA (bonded cellular) support' to a fork of rstular/srt-live-server, and carries no license statement in the README
options.androidSupport: n/a
options.verdict: DO NOT USE without a provenance audit. An MIT label on a repo that implements SRTLA — whose only reference implementation is AGPL-3.0 — is a claim to verify, not to rely on. If any srtla-derived code is in there, the MIT grant is ineffective and you inherit the AGPL problem on your own relay.

hardConstraints: LICENSE — srtla is AGPL-3.0, full stop. LICENSE header: 'GNU AFFERO GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE Version 3, 19 November 2007'; GitHub SPDX agpl-3.0. Two separate infections: (a) shipping srtla_send inside the Electron app or the APK is *distribution* of AGPL code, which requires the entire combined work be offered under AGPL — LIVETAP stops being MIT; (b) running a *modified* srtla_rec on the LIVETAP relay triggers AGPL §13's network clause, which requires offering Corresponding Source to every remote user interacting with it. Note the §13 nuance: the network obligation fires only if you modify the program. You will modify it. Nobody runs stock srtla_rec in production. https://github.com/BELABOX/srtla/blob/main/LICENSE

LICENSE — SRT, libdatachannel and every serious QUIC library are safe; WireGuard's kernel/NT code is not. MPL-2.0 (SRT, libdatachannel ≥0.18) is file-level copyleft: Mozilla FAQ Q11 — 'new files containing no MPL-licensed code are not Modifications, and therefore do not need to be distributed under the terms of the MPL' — and Q13 confirms combining with BSD/Apache in one executable. Safe to statically link into MIT LIVETAP; you only publish edits to MPL files. Clean permissive: quiche BSD-2-Clause, msquic MIT, picoquic MIT, lsquic MIT, quinn MIT-OR-Apache-2.0, mvfst MIT, libsodium ISC, OpenSSL 3.0+ Apache-2.0, BoringSSL Apache-2.0 (relicensed Feb 2025), RootEncoder Apache-2.0. Poison: WireGuard kernel module and wireguard-nt are GPL-2.0. wireguard-go (MIT) and BoringTun (BSD-3) are the usable WireGuard-family code.

PROTOCOL — SRT's own bonding cannot aggregate capacity in production. Haivision's socket-groups doc: broadcast mode means 'The payload sent for a group will be then sent over every single link in the group simultaneously' and 'every next link in this group gives then another 100% overhead'. Backup mode is failover, not aggregation. Balancing — the only mode that actually shares bandwidth — is marked 'UNDER DEVELOPMENT', is 'not directly used as protection', and lacks automatic recovery for broken links. Multicast is 'CONCEPT! NOT IMPLEMENTED!'. If you plan to ship SRT bonding and skip srtla, you are shipping a failover product and calling it bonding. https://github.com/Haivision/srt/blob/master/docs/features/socket-groups.md

STANDARDS — Multipath QUIC is not an RFC yet. draft-ietf-quic-multipath-21, dated 17 March 2026, expires 18 September 2026 (three days from today). WG state 'Submitted to IESG for Publication', IESG state 'Waiting for AD Go-Ahead::AD Followup'. There is no RFC number to cite in a spec, and the wire format can still move. msquic maintainers state there is no multipath support and no official timeline — only an unreviewed external draft PR. https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-quic-multipath • https://github.com/microsoft/msquic/discussions/4890

iOS — Apple forbids aggregate multipath in App Store apps. NWParameters.MultipathServiceType.aggregate 'aggregates the capacities of other Multipath options in an attempt to increase throughput', but Apple does not allow aggregate mode in production apps; it is reachable only via the Developer Settings screen on a developer device. Production apps are limited to .handover and .interactive — both of which are failover/latency modes, not capacity aggregation — and even those require the com.apple.developer.networking.multipath entitlement enabled in Xcode Capabilities. CONSEQUENCE: an iOS LIVETAP Bond can never use OS-level multipath for bonding. It must implement its own UDP multipath in-app, opening one socket per interface via NWParameters.requiredInterfaceType = .cellular / .wifi. That is permitted — but it means the iOS client is a from-scratch build, not a configuration flag. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/network/nwparameters/multipathservicetype-swift.enum/aggregate • https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/entitlements/com.apple.developer.networking.multipath

ANDROID — simultaneous Wi-Fi + cellular works and is documented, with three specific gotchas. Google's own docs: 'An Android-powered device can maintain many connections at the same time', and 'Apps with this permission let the system try to bring up a network that isn't up, such as the mobile network when the device is connected to a Wi-Fi network.' (1) That permission is CHANGE_NETWORK_STATE — required, and the docs warn 'Most apps don't need to use additional networks'. (2) HARD LIMIT: the system caps outstanding requests at 100 per UID, shared across all requestNetwork and registerNetworkCallback variants; exceeding it throws TooManyRequestsException. A path manager that re-requests on every flap will hit this — you must unregisterNetworkCallback rigorously. (3) Bind per-path with Network.bindSocket() (socket must not be connected) rather than bindProcessToNetwork(), which Google explicitly advises against. https://developer.android.com/develop/connectivity/network-ops/reading-network-state

ANDROID 14+ — foreground service type is a shipping gate, not a detail. Targeting API 34+ you must declare a foreground service type in the manifest, request the matching FOREGROUND_SERVICE_<TYPE> permission alongside FOREGROUND_SERVICE, *and* declare it in Play Console (App content → Foreground service types) or the release is blocked. For LIVETAP that is likely mediaProjection and/or dataSync (dataSync explicitly covers 'transferring data locally or over a network'). Also: you cannot start a foreground service from the background except via documented exemptions (FCM high-priority, alarm, user-initiated job). A bonding manager that tries to resurrect a dropped stream from the background will silently fail. https://developer.android.com/about/versions/14/changes/fgs-types-required • https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/13392821

CRYPTO — DTLS 1.3 is not shippable on OpenSSL today. OpenSSL's own announcement (9 Sep 2026): 'OpenSSL 4.1, which will be released in October 2026, adds the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol version 1.3.' Only 4.1.0-alpha1 exists right now. Migration caveat straight from the post: 'DTLSv1_listen() does not support DTLS 1.3' — you must move to SSL_new_listener(). The only mature DTLS 1.3 (including full Connection ID) is wolfSSL, which is dual-licensed GPLv2-or-commercial — verify this before linking, because GPLv2 would infect MIT LIVETAP exactly the way srtla does. https://openssl-library.org/post/2026-09-09-dtls-1.3/

CRYPTO — DTLS 1.2 + Connection ID disqualifies itself for multipath. RFC 9146 §8: 'The lack of a CID update mechanism in DTLS 1.2 makes this extension unsuitable for mobility scenarios where correlation must be considered,' and the RFC says implementers SHOULD refuse to use CIDs in DTLS 1.2 and switch to DTLS 1.3. It also names your exact scenario: in multihoming an adversary can 'correlate the communication interaction over the two paths'. Plain DTLS without CID is worse — it identifies connections by the 5-tuple and has no connection migration at all, so every path change kills the session. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9146.html

SECURITY — srtla's path-join is an unauthenticated bearer token, and copying its design would be a vulnerability. From srtla_send.c: the group id is 16 bytes (SRTLA_ID_LEN) read from /dev/urandom, sent in cleartext in SRTLA_REG1. A new link is admitted if only the FIRST HALF matches: `if (memcmp(id, srtla_id, SRTLA_ID_LEN/2) != 0)`. So an on-path observer who sees one REG1 packet learns the 8 bytes needed to register additional links into a live broadcast group. There is no cryptographic authentication of path membership — the code has a syn_cookie field and an enc_field, but neither authenticates a joining link. Do not reimplement this shape. https://github.com/BELABOX/srtla/blob/main/srtla_send.c

SECURITY — a multipath relay invites six attack classes a single TCP+TLS connection does not. (1) PATH INJECTION: any bearer-token path-join lets an attacker add a link and inject or observe (srtla, above). Fix: derive path-add authorization from the session key — QUIC issues connection IDs under encryption and validates with PATH_CHALLENGE/PATH_RESPONSE (RFC 9000 §8.2). (2) REFLECTION/AMPLIFICATION: every unvalidated address is a new amplification vector; RFC 9000 §8.1 caps sending at 3x bytes received from an unvalidated address for exactly this reason. RFC 9146 §9 notes peers cannot distinguish genuine NAT rebinding from a spoofed update, and attackers can 'replay datagrams with modified IP addresses / port numbers'. (3) REPLAY: one global sequence window across N paths is wrong — it either false-rejects legitimate cross-path reordering or accepts replays. DTLS 1.3 (RFC 9147) mandates a separate sliding window per epoch, borrowed from RFC 4303 §3.4.3; multipath QUIC gives each path its own packet number space. Copy that. (4) LINKABILITY: a stable identifier visible on every path lets a passive observer bind the user's home IP to their phone's cellular identity — you would be publishing 'these two addresses are the same person.' RFC 9000 §9.5 requires fresh connection IDs per path to prevent exactly this. (5) RELAY IMPERSONATION: RTMPS to YouTube authenticates the server by PKI; a custom UDP relay has no such thing by default. Without a pinned relay static public key, a DNS or BGP hijack silently MITMs the stream and captures the stream key. (6) SCHEDULER STARVATION: a path that ACKs but never delivers causes head-of-line blocking at reassembly — per-path congestion state and aggressive path eviction are mandatory, not optional.

CRYPTO — SRT's passphrase encryption is not sufficient authentication for a relay. SRT uses AES-CTR (128/192/256) with a Stream Encrypting Key wrapped by a Key Encrypting Key derived from a shared passphrase via PBKDF2. There is no ephemeral key exchange, therefore no forward secrecy: compromise the passphrase and an attacker derives the KEK and unwraps every past and future SEK for that session. It also authenticates nothing about *who* the relay is — a passphrase is a symmetric shared secret, so anyone holding it can impersonate the relay to the client. KM Refresh Rate / KM Pre-Announce limit exposure per-SEK but do not fix either problem. https://github.com/Haivision/srt/blob/master/docs/features/encryption.md

COST — a bonded stream can eat a month of cellular allowance in under an hour, and the failure mode is silent. Arithmetic: 6 Mbps sustained = 2.7 GB/hour; a 3-hour IRL stream mostly on cellular ≈ 8 GB. Speedify — the closest commercial analogue — defaults to a 2 GB/month and 200 MB/day cellular cap with a warning at 75%, and deliberately sets cellular to 'Normal' priority so Wi-Fi is preferred whenever fast enough. That default budget is smaller than a single hour of LIVETAP at 6 Mbps. The structural danger: when Wi-Fi degrades mid-broadcast, an aggregating scheduler silently migrates the FULL bitrate to cellular with no user-visible event. And if you ever ship SRT-style redundancy, broadcast mode doubles it outright. https://support.speedify.com/article/344-data-limits • https://support.speedify.com/article/950-over-data-plan

CARRIER POLICY — no law blocks this, but carrier AUPs arguably do, and tethering is capped hard. Carrier acceptable-use policies prohibit 'continuous, unattended, or excessive streaming, downloading, or uploading of videos, music, or other files' and applications 'designed for unattended use... that degrades network capacity'. A multi-hour bonded upload is squarely in that language's blast radius. Separately: 'unlimited' plans carry a premium-data threshold (commonly 5/50/100 GB) after which traffic is deprioritized during congestion — the exact moment a live broadcast cannot absorb it. And the tether/hotspot path LIVETAP Bond names as a first-class link is the weakest: typical plans allow 10–50 GB of high-speed hotspot data then throttle to ~600 kbps or even 128 kbps. Never let the scheduler count tether as durable capacity. https://www.verizon.com/about/terms-conditions/acceptable-use-policy • https://www.whistleout.com/CellPhones/Guides/does-unlimited-data-mean-unlimited-hotspot

THERMAL — the encoder and the radios compete, and throttling looks exactly like network loss. Android exposes the problem via PowerManager.addThermalStatusListener(), getThermalHeadroom(int) and THERMAL_STATUS_SEVERE (headroom 1.0 = throttled at severe), plus the NDK android/thermal.h group. AOSP is explicit that sustained performance requires OEM power-HAL changes to lock max CPU/GPU frequencies, and that thermal pressure may limit 'CPU, GPU, display, charging, or other subsystems' — radios included. Published measurement of the shape: recent flagships lose ~27% throughput within three iterations of sustained load as they enter thermal limitation. THE DESIGN HAZARD: LIVETAP already runs a hardware encoder at high bitrate; add two hot radios and a lit screen and you are at the worst thermal case a phone has. When throttling hits the encoder, output bitrate drops — and a naive bonding scheduler will misread that as network degradation and start shifting paths, making things worse. Feed thermal status into the scheduler explicitly. https://source.android.com/docs/core/power/performance • https://developer.android.com/games/optimize/adpf/thermal
report.recommendation:
Do not touch srtla — not the client, not the relay, not a "clean-room" port written by anyone who has read it. It is AGPL-3.0 and it is also cryptographically unsound (8-byte cleartext bearer token admits new paths into a live group). Treat the existence of srtla as market validation, not as a component.

Build LIVETAP Bond as multipath-QUIC-shaped. Prototype on picoquic (MIT, the reference multipath implementation) and evaluate quiche (BSD-2, better maintained, verify its multipath state against the current tree). Both are license-clean for MIT. Accept that draft-ietf-quic-multipath is not an RFC yet: pin a draft version, version your wire format, and own both ends — you control the client and the relay, so you are not chasing interop.

If QUIC multipath proves too heavy for the Android/iOS builds, the fallback is a small custom UDP protocol whose crypto you do not invent: Noise IK via libsodium (ISC), copying WireGuard's construction (Noise_IKpsk2, ChaCha20-Poly1305, 1-RTT, relay's static public key pinned in the app binary). That pinning simultaneously solves relay authentication — the thing a passphrase-based scheme like SRT's cannot do. Then borrow three specific mechanisms from RFC 9000 rather than improvising them: per-path packet number spaces, PATH_CHALLENGE/PATH_RESPONSE before a path carries payload, and the 3x anti-amplification cap on unvalidated addresses. Use SRT (MPL-2.0) only relay→CDN, never for bonding.

Ship cellular as backup-first, not aggregate-first. Default the scheduler to prefer NET_CAPABILITY_NOT_METERED paths; require an explicit opt-in per broadcast to let cellular carry capacity; enforce a hard byte budget in the scheduler itself, not a warning banner; and put a live "cellular carried X MB this session" readout in the Studio UI. 2.7 GB/hour is not a number a user discovers on their bill.

Plan for iOS being a separate build, not a port. Apple will not let an App Store app use OS aggregate multipath, so the in-app per-interface socket approach is the only route — and it is the same approach Android needs anyway via requestNetwork + bindSocket. That symmetry is an argument for writing the path manager yourself in portable C/Rust and keeping the platform layer thin.

Two things to verify before writing code: (1) audit irl-srt-server's SRTLA code provenance against AGPL srtla — its MIT label is a claim, not a guarantee; (2) confirm wolfSSL's license terms if DTLS 1.3 tempts you, because OpenSSL's DTLS 1.3 is not released until October 2026 and the mature alternative is GPLv2-or-commercial.
uncertainties: No credible public measurement exists (that I could find) for the incremental power draw of Wi-Fi TX and cellular TX running simultaneously at sustained multi-Mbps uplink. The thermal-throttling literature describes the shape of the problem but not this specific workload. This is a gap you must close by measuring on your own target hardware — it is an unknown, not a documented constraint.

cloudflare/quiche's current multipath status could not be pinned down. Its source contains a PathMap for multi-path management, but I found no release note or doc confirming draft-ietf-quic-multipath conformance, and no evidence of removal either. Read the tree before betting on it.

wolfSSL's GPLv2-or-commercial dual license is stated from general knowledge, not from a page I fetched in this pass. Verify directly before linking it — if it is GPLv2, it is as dangerous to MIT LIVETAP as srtla is.

irl-srt-server reports MIT via the GitHub API, but its README carries no license statement and it advertises SRTLA support inherited into a fork of srt-live-server. Whether its SRTLA implementation is independent or srtla-derived determines whether the MIT grant is even valid. This needs a code-level diff against BELABOX/srtla, not a badge check.

draft-ietf-quic-multipath-21 expires 18 September 2026 — three days after this report. It may be replaced by a -22 or published as an RFC imminently. Re-check the datatracker before freezing a wire format.

Carrier AUP language prohibiting 'continuous, unattended, or excessive' uploading is real and quoted, but I found no evidence of a carrier actually terminating a bonded-streaming customer. The enforcement risk is plausible-but-unproven; the deprioritization and hotspot-throttle risks are certain and are the ones that will actually degrade broadcasts.

Whether Android devices reliably keep the cellular radio up alongside Wi-Fi is device- and OEM-dependent in practice. The API contract is documented and clear; real-world behavior across the Android fleet (especially with Data Saver or OEM battery managers active) needs a device-matrix test.

Prototype on picoquic (MIT, the reference multipath implementation) and evaluate quiche (BSD-2, better maintained, verify its multipath state against the current tree)... If QUIC multipath proves too heavy for the Android/iOS builds, the fallback is a small custom UDP protocol... Noise IK via libsodium... Plan for iOS being a separate build, not a port... verdict.reasoning:
Six independent problems, three of them disqualifying.

(1) QUICHE HAS NO MULTIPATH — it is not a "verify the state" item, it is absent. quiche 0.29.3 README/docs.rs mention multipath nowhere (https://docs.rs/crate/quiche/latest/source/README.md). The QUIC WG's own roster records quiche's multipath as "currently work-in-progress as a PR" on a fork at draft-12, page last updated Feb 2025, while the draft is now -21 (https://github.com/quicwg/multipath/wiki/QUIC-Implementations-with-multipath-support). TQUIC's comparison table marks QUICHE-CF multipath "Not supported" (https://tquic.net/docs/further_readings/comparison/). cloudflare/quiche#278 (multipath request, opened 2019) is closed with no implementation. Half the recommended prototyping plan is a library that cannot do the thing.

(2) PICOQUIC HAS NO MOBILE STORY AND CALLS STANDARD MULTIPATH "PLANNED". Its README verifies builds on "Windows, Linux, MacOS (Intel and M1), and FreeBSD" — no Android, no iOS — and lists "support for the standard version of multipath" under *planned developments*, alongside a "simple multipath alternative" that is not the IETF wire format. It also drags in picotls + OpenSSL 1.1.1/3.0 as a hard dependency (https://github.com/private-octopus/picoquic). Betting an Android-APK-and-iOS product on cross-compiling a research C stack with no shipped mobile target is the single largest unpriced risk in the plan. The implementations that actually have multipath today and were never evaluated: TQUIC (Rust, Apache-2.0, Tencent) and xquic (C, Alibaba).

(3) MP-QUIC EXPLICITLY REFUSES TO GIVE YOU THE ONE THING BONDING IS. The draft states: "This document does not specify scheduling algorithms that define how multiple, simultaneously open paths are used to send packets" (https://quicwg.org/multipath/draft-ietf-quic-multipath.html). The scheduler IS the product. Worse, the only published real-time-video MPQUIC measurement — MoMQ, built on TQUIC, not picoquic or quiche — finds transport-layer schedulers are frame-blind ("treats the application-layer packets as uniform bytes and decides from transport metrics alone"), yielding P99.9 frame completion of 384.7 ms with the best stock scheduler, and, decisively for your cost model, drives metered-path usage to 90–100% (https://arxiv.org/html/2608.10741). "Default the scheduler to prefer NET_CAPABILITY_NOT_METERED" is not a knob on an off-the-shelf MPQUIC stack; it is code you write, after paying QUIC's weight for connection IDs and PATH_CHALLENGE you could have implemented directly.

(4) THE iOS CONCLUSION IS REFUTED BY A SHIPPING APP STORE APP. Moblin — MIT licensed, on the App Store as id6466745933 — README: "Can use one cellular, one WiFi and multiple Ethernet connections simultaneously. Often called bonding," implemented in Swift, with SRTLA and RIST, no multipath entitlement (https://github.com/eerimoq/moblin). iOS bonding is not an unproven from-scratch build; it is the incumbent, MIT-licensed, and readable. Apple DTS confirms the mechanism: Matt Eaton, "If you are using a low level networking API with TCP or UDP then you could take a look at requiredInterfaceType on NWConnection... params.requiredInterfaceType = .cellular; params.prohibitedInterfaceTypes = [.wifi]" (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/671756). Caveat worth carrying: Quinn (Apple DTS) warns forced-interface attempts can be blocked by NECP policy (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/795079), and getaddrinfo does not work with scoped networks — resolve inside Network.framework.

(5) RIST IS MISSING FROM THE ANALYSIS ENTIRELY, AND IT IS THE PERMISSIVE, PUBLISHED, SHIPPING OPTION. RIST is a published VSF standard (TR-06-1:2020, TR-06-2), not an expiring draft; Main Profile includes bonding with load sharing where "the sender may split the packets across multiple interfaces/paths/ISP/delivery methods" (https://www.rist.tv/articles-and-deep-dives/2020/6/16/rist-bonding-and-load-sharing-demystified). librist is BSD-2-Clause — confirmed from COPYING, "Copyright © 2019-2020, VideoLAN and librist authors", SPDX BSD-2-Clause — royalty-free, patent-royalty-free, "no external runtime dependencies on any OS other than normal core OS libraries" (https://github.com/deepin-community/librist/blob/master/README.md). Main Profile's DTLS + x.509 solves relay authentication with PKI, which is strictly better than the plan's single hardcoded static key: pin one leaf key in the binary and an emergency rotation costs an App Store review cycle. Honest caveats: librist's bonding modes are "broadcast" (duplicate) and "round-robin" (even split), not capacity-weighted — so you still write the scheduler — and tunnel-level multipath is an open librist issue (#47), so Main Profile tunneling and multipath are not yet composed.

(6) ANDROID ANALYSIS STOPS AT 14 AND MISSES THE 15 GATE. The plan names dataSync as the likely FGS type. Android 15+: "The system permits dataSync and mediaProcessing foreground services to run for a total of 6 hours in a 24-hour period," then Service.onTimeout() fires, you have seconds to stopSelf(), else android.app.RemoteServiceException "A foreground service of type [type] did not stop within its timeout"; a restart throws ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException "Time limit already exhausted for foreground service type dataSync" (https://developer.android.com/develop/background-work/services/fgs/timeout). Google further states dataSync "will be deprecated" and directs network transfers to user-initiated data transfer jobs, which must be "directly prompted by the user" and "only operate for the duration required" (https://developer.android.com/develop/background-work/background-tasks/data-transfer-options). camera, microphone and mediaProjection are the exempt types — so the bonding manager must live inside the capture FGS, not its own dataSync service. That is an architecture constraint, not a manifest line.

(7) THE CUSTOM-CRYPTO FALLBACK HAS AN UNPRICED REGULATORY TAIL. Shipping your own bulk-encryption transport is non-exempt encryption: Apple requires export compliance documentation, BIS requires an annual self-classification report due 1 February under the ERN framework, and "proprietary encryption algorithms not accepted by international standard bodies (such as IEEE, IETF, or ITU)" require CCATS (https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/reference/app-information/export-compliance-documentation-for-encryption/). A standard protocol (QUIC/TLS, DTLS, RIST Main Profile) is materially cheaper here than "a small custom UDP protocol."

(8) THE srtla PROHIBITION IS OVER-BROAD IN ONE SPECIFIC WAY. The AGPL-3.0 finding is confirmed (LICENSE fetched: "GNU AFFERO GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE / Version 3, 19 November 2007"). But "not even a clean-room port written by anyone who has read it" conflates code with wire format. Moblin's MIT-licensed Swift SRTLA implementation ships on the App Store; speaking the protocol is not the infringing act, copying the source is. Refusing SRTLA interop on the relay throws away drop-in compatibility with the entire installed BELABOX/Moblin base — the market the plan calls "validation." The 8-byte-prefix token critique is a reason not to copy srtla's *design*, not a reason to refuse to *accept* srtla senders at the relay behind your own auth.

WHAT SURVIVES: SRT socket-groups cannot aggregate (correct); srtla is AGPL (correct); the RFC 9000 mechanisms named (per-path PN spaces, PATH_CHALLENGE/RESPONSE, 3x anti-amplification) are the right primitives; a hard cellular byte budget enforced in the scheduler is correct and MoMQ's 90–100% metered-path finding makes it urgent, not optional. Also confirmed as a genuinely closed door: MPTCP is not an Android fallback — mainline Linux has IPPROTO_MPTCP (262) since 5.6, but Android MPTCP remains research ports to Nexus-era devices with no supported app-level socket (https://multipath-tcp.org/pmwiki.php/Users/Android). Draft status unchanged and still unsafe to cite: draft-ietf-quic-multipath-21, IESG "Waiting for AD Go-Ahead::AD Followup", no RFC number, -21 expires 18 Sept 2026 — and the WG's interop page is pinned to draft-04 and last edited July 2024, so the ecosystem is thinner than the draft number implies.
verdict.correction: Drop quiche from the plan — it has no multipath in any released version. Drop picoquic as the primary prototype — no Android/iOS build target, standard multipath still "planned," OpenSSL dependency. Run two prototypes instead: (A) librist (BSD-2-Clause, VSF TR-06-1/TR-06-2, DTLS+x.509 for relay identity, already shipping on iOS via Moblin) with your own capacity-weighted scheduler replacing librist's round-robin; (B) if you insist on QUIC-shaped, prototype on TQUIC (Rust, Apache-2.0) — the stack the only published real-time-video MPQUIC study actually used — not picoquic or quiche. Either way, write the scheduler yourself: the MP-QUIC draft explicitly declines to specify one, and stock transport schedulers push 90–100% of traffic onto metered paths. Pin a relay ROOT key and sign short-lived leaf keys, never a single static leaf in the binary, or key rotation costs an App Store review. Put the Android bonding manager inside the camera/microphone foreground service — dataSync is capped at 6h/24h under Android 15 and is slated for deprecation. Treat iOS as a proven pattern with an MIT reference (Moblin), not a from-scratch build. Keep the srtla code ban; lift the srtla protocol ban and let the relay accept SRTLA senders behind your own authentication, for installed-base compatibility. And budget for export-compliance filings (Apple declaration + annual BIS self-classification) the moment you ship any bulk-encryption transport of your own.
